A01.q: Your rough cut about a Varanasi weaver whose trade is dying gives equal time to her, a mall owner, a tourist and an official. Test viewers call it informative but flat. What do you do?
options: Choose whose experience the film lives inside, and rebuild the cut around her, using the others only where they touch her life.
Add two more interviews so every side of the issue is covered, and balance all six voices' screen time exactly.
More balance makes it even flatter, because the viewer still has no one to stand with.
Keep the four voices but shorten each interview, so the pace feels faster and the film no longer drags in the middle.
Pace isn't the problem; the film has no point of view.
Open with the official and the mall owner for context, then turn to the weaver once the facts are set.
Facts first keeps it informative; the weaver stays one voice among four.
A01.why: Flatness comes from refusing to take a side. Anchoring the film in one person's experience gives the viewer something to feel.

A01.q: In the framing choices section, how does StudioBinder link composition to the film's outlook?
options: Where the camera sits and what the frame shows or hides tell the viewer whose side to feel and how.
Composition mainly keeps the frame balanced and pleasing, and the film's outlook comes from the script.
The video shows framing doing story work, not just making pretty pictures.
Wide, neutral frames suit most scenes, and close framing is saved only for big action moments.
The video treats every framing choice as a statement, not a rule about shot size.
The outlook is decided in the edit; framing only needs to give the editor safe coverage.
Framing already decides what the viewer feels.
A01.why: Framing is never neutral. Each choice of angle, distance and what is left out pushes the viewer toward a way of seeing.
A01.video: Cinematic Film Composition — Blocking, Staging & Composition

A01.q: In the Sundance session, Roger Ross Williams talks about finding your view and then your visual style. What order does that suggest?
options: Work out what you personally believe about the subject first, then let the look of the film grow from it.
Pick a strong visual style first, then find a subject and story that suit that look.
Style chosen first often feels like decoration with nothing behind it.
Stay neutral while filming, then decide what the film believes once you reach the edit.
Without a view in the field you often miss the shots that would carry it.
Pick a visual style and a belief together on the first shoot day, once you have seen the location and the people.
A view of the subject should come before filming, not from the location.
A01.why: The look of a documentary works best when it expresses the filmmaker's stance, so the stance has to come first.
A01.video: Documentary: Finding and Shaping Your Story

A01.q: In a brand film for a Jaipur bakery, the owner says early on that her grandmother's recipe failed for years. The film ends on a montage of happy customers. Viewers say the ending feels empty. What is the best fix?
options: End on the moment she finally gets the recipe right, so the problem raised at the start gets its answer.
Move the customer montage earlier and add a warm voiceover summing up what the bakery stands for.
A summary explains the film but still leaves the opening question hanging.
Cut her line about the failed recipe so the film no longer leaves anything unresolved.
This removes the hook that gave the viewer a reason to keep watching.
Add a title card before the montage telling viewers the recipe now works.
Telling the answer instead of showing it leaves the ending empty.
A01.why: The opening line set up a question. The ending feels empty because it never answers it.

A01.q: Editing a wedding film, you have the bride's father saying in the first minute that he is sure he won't cry. Later you have him wiping his eyes at the bidaai. How do you use these?
options: Keep his line near the start and hold the tearful shot for the closing stretch of the film.
Cut straight from his line to the tearful shot so the funny contrast lands right away.
Paying it off at once wastes the tension that could carry the whole film.
Drop his line from the film, since the family might find it embarrassing to watch.
Without the line, the tears lose the meaning that makes them land so hard.
Place the tearful shot early and his line near the end, so the joke lands as a reveal.
The set-up has to come first for the payoff to work.
A01.why: An early statement makes the viewer wait for the answer. Holding the payoff till the end gives the film a spine.

A01.q: You are making a film about a Kerala family selling their ancestral house. You filmed the front door at many points across the shoot. How do you use these shots?
options: Bring the door back at a few key moments: open for guests, later locked, finally a stranger's hand on it.
Pick the single most beautiful door shot and use it once as a strong opening image.
Used once, the door is just a nice shot and never builds meaning.
Use the door opening and closing as a transition between scenes all through the film, in every act.
As a mechanical transition it becomes a device, not something the viewer feels.
Use the door only at the start and the end, framed identically.
Two bookends don't build; the door needs to change in between.
A01.why: When the door returns in a new state, it carries the memory of earlier scenes, so each return says more.

A01.q: In a short film about a mother, a pressure cooker whistle is heard in several scenes. Your editor wants to remove it from the later scenes because it feels repetitive. What do you say?
options: Keep a few returns, placed where it means something new, like a whistle in the empty kitchen after she is gone.
Agree, and keep it only in the very first scene so the sound does not become tiring or predictable for your viewers.
Cutting the returns throws away the meaning the sound could build over the film.
Keep it in every scene at the same level so the sound stays steady and familiar throughout.
Unchanged repetition does feel tiring, because the sound never means anything new.
Replace the whistle with music in the later scenes to avoid repetition.
The repeated sound is what builds meaning; music removes it.
A01.why: A returning sound earns its place when each return lands in a new context and adds feeling.

A01.q: You are cutting a calm, gentle film for a hospice in Pune. The client asks for an upbeat stock track and fast cuts in the middle donor-appeal section. What do you do?
options: Explain that a sudden shift will jar viewers, and offer a lift that fits, like warmer music and a hopeful face.
Do it as asked, since the client knows their donors better than you, has the final say and is paying for the film.
You are hired for your judgement, and a jarring section can lose the very donors they want.
Make the whole film more upbeat so the donor section no longer stands out from the rest.
This fixes the jump by throwing away the feeling that suits the subject.
Refuse the request and tell the client the donor section will stay as it is.
Refusing ignores the client's goal; offer a fitting alternative.
A01.why: An unplanned change in feeling breaks trust with the viewer. A good lift works inside the film's mood.

A01.q: In Robin Piree's section on what to write in a director's treatment, what job does the treatment do for the feel of the film?
options: It puts the intended feeling into words and reference images before the shoot, so crew and client share it.
It is mainly a schedule and budget document that the producer uses to plan the shoot days.
That is a production plan, not the creative vision the video describes.
It is written after the edit to describe the finished film when pitching it to festivals.
The treatment comes before the shoot, to guide the choices that create the feel.
It is a legal agreement between the director and the producer about who controls the main creative decisions.
A treatment shares the feeling and style; it isn't a contract.
A01.why: Writing down image, feeling and execution early lets everyone make small choices that point the same way.
A01.video: How To Write A Director's Treatment (FAST)?

A01.q: Your two-minute portrait of a Kolkata tabla teacher runs 40 seconds long. You have two moving answers about his guru that say the same thing, and a gorgeous drone shot of Howrah Bridge that has nothing to do with him. What do you do?
options: Keep the stronger of the two guru answers and drop the bridge shot, even though it looks great.
Keep both guru answers and the bridge shot, and trim the pauses between his lines instead.
Cutting his pauses removes breathing room while keeping material that repeats or distracts.
Keep everything and speed up the B-roll, the supporting shots, so the whole film fits two minutes.
Rushing every shot weakens the whole film instead of choosing what matters.
Keep both guru answers and cut the drone shot, even though the answers say the same thing.
Two answers that say the same thing weaken each other.
A01.why: Repeated points and pretty but unrelated shots dilute a short film. Removing them makes the rest hit harder.

A01.q: In a film about a farmer after a crop failure, you have him explaining his debts in detail, and a long shot of him silently staring at his dry field. How do you shape this moment?
options: Let the silent shot carry the moment and cut most of the explanation, trusting the viewer to feel it.
Keep the full explanation so no viewer misses any of the facts about his situation.
Too much explaining talks over the feeling the silent shot could deliver.
Put on-screen text with his debt amount over the silent shot so both work together.
Adding text explains what the image already says and breaks the silence.
Keep a short version of the explanation, and play it as voiceover over the silent shot of the field.
The explanation would still compete with the silence.
A01.why: What the viewer works out for themselves often lands deeper than what they are told.

A01.q: Your short film about a Lucknow girl learning to ride a cycle opens with her watching other kids ride past her doorway. Which closing shot works best?
options: The same doorway framing, but now she rides past it while a younger child watches from the step.
A new scene of her family celebrating with sweets around the dinner table at home later that evening.
A brand new setting at the end feels nice but does not connect back to where we began.
A fade to black right after the moment she first manages to stay balanced.
Stopping at the moment of success feels abrupt and gives the viewer no sense of the full journey.
A close-up of her smiling proudly at the camera as she rides.
A new framing loses the echo of the opening doorway.
A01.why: Returning to the first image with her role reversed lets the viewer feel how far she has come.

A01.q: A brand film for a roadside chai stall opens at dawn with the owner lighting his stove. How do you close it?
options: At night, from the same angle, he turns the stove off, with the day's used cups piled around him.
Repeat the exact dawn shot of him lighting the stove, so the film neatly comes full circle.
An exact repeat shows nothing has happened, so the viewer feels no journey.
End on a happy customer praising the taste of his chai straight to the camera.
A testimonial adds a new voice at the end instead of completing his day.
Repeat the dawn shot, but at dusk, with him lighting the stove again for the night.
The same action shows no change; the ending needs a different feeling.
A01.why: Mirroring the first shot, now marked by a full day's work, gives the film shape and a sense of time passed.

A02.q: A producer pitches you a film about boat families on the ghats of Varanasi. Before you book a crew, what do you do first?
options: Spend a few days with several families, camera packed away, learning who opens up and what is really happening.
Film the first family you meet on day one, so you catch their fresh and honest reactions.
Filming before you understand the people often locks you into the wrong subject and the wrong story.
Write a full script from news articles first, then look for families who fit the parts you have written.
This forces real people into a story you guessed, instead of finding the one that is actually there.
Ask the local boat union to choose the families, then film all of them in the first week.
The union decides who is seen, and filming at once skips the slow work of earning trust.
A02.why: Time with people, without the pressure of a camera, shows you who is open, who holds the screen, and what story the place really has. Only then do you commit crew and money.

A02.q: In the research chapter, what key question is early research meant to answer?
options: Whether the subject and the access you have can carry a full-length film.
Which camera, lenses and sound kit will suit the story best.
Gear choices come later and are not what this research stage is testing.
How to cut a strong trailer to win money from funders.
A trailer may follow, but the research is about whether the film can exist at all.
Which funders will back the film, and what they will want to see in it first.
Funding follows once you know the subject can carry the film.
A02.why: Research tests if the people and your access are deep enough to hold up a whole film before you spend on production.
A02.video: Documentary: Finding and Shaping Your Story

A02.q: An old mill owner in Kanpur tells you on camera that his mill employed 5,000 workers in 1980. You want to use this in narration. What do you do?
options: Find an original record, like union or company files, confirm it with a second source, and log both.
Use the number as it is, because he ran the mill for many decades and clearly knows his own history best.
Memories fade and people round up, so a first-hand claim still needs checking.
Add the word "reportedly" to the narration and move on, without checking it any further.
A soft word does not protect you if the number is wrong, and it weakens trust in the film.
Ask two former workers whether it sounds right, and use it if they agree.
Memories can agree and still be wrong; use records.
A02.why: An original document plus a second source makes the claim solid, and logging them means you can prove it later.

A02.q: Weeks into the edit, the broadcaster's legal team asks where a statistic in your film came from. What would make this an easy answer?
options: A running sheet linking each claim to its source, the date found, and who checked it.
Searching your browser history to find the article you read during your research.
History gets cleared and links break, so this is slow and often fails.
Phoning the interviewee and asking them to confirm the number once more.
Asking the same person again is not an independent source and proves nothing new.
A shared folder with every article and PDF you saved, without labels.
Without labels no one can tell which file supports which claim.
A02.why: Keeping a sheet as you go means every claim has a trail ready for legal review.

A02.q: The owner of a small textile workshop in Surat asks, "Will I get to approve the final film?" You cannot offer that. What do you say?
options: Tell her plainly she won't have final say, but explain the film's angle and where it will be shown.
Say yes for now, since you need the access and can sort out the details later.
A false promise breaks trust when it surfaces and can lead to legal trouble.
Avoid the question, and get the release form signed quickly before she starts to worry more.
Consent gained by dodging questions is not real consent and can collapse later.
Say you will take her notes seriously, without saying who has final say.
A vague promise leads to a dispute later.
A02.why: Clear limits plus a true picture of the film and its audience build trust that lasts through release.

A02.q: Why does the talk stress making ethical choices before production begins?
options: Choices about consent and fairness shape trust and are hard to fix once filming starts.
Ethics is mainly a legal step that you can finish after the edit is locked.
By then any harm or broken trust has already happened during the shoot.
Subjects act more naturally when they know less about what the film is about.
Keeping people in the dark damages consent and trust, which the talk treats as central.
Rules vary by country, so they are best learned once you know where it will air.
Fairness and consent guide choices from the start.
A02.why: Deciding early how you will treat and talk with subjects sets fair terms that guide the whole shoot.
A02.video: Documentary Filmmaking: Navigating Truth and Ethics

A02.q: Halfway through a film on a Kerala football club, the star player is injured and a young reserve becomes the real heart of the story. What do you do?
options: Rework your scene list around the reserve, keeping earlier scenes that still serve the new arc.
Stick to the planned scenes and the star player, since the funder already approved the original story.
Ignoring the stronger story leaves you with a film that no longer matches reality.
Drop planning altogether and just follow whatever happens on each shoot day.
Without a plan you will miss key moments and end up with footage that doesn't connect.
Add the reserve as a side thread and keep the injured star as the main arc.
The heart of the story has moved, and the arc must follow.
A02.why: A good plan bends to what you discover, so you keep structure while chasing the better story.

A02.q: A brand client hiring you for an unscripted documentary asks to see "the script" before the shoot. How do you respond?
options: Share a list of the moments you expect to capture, and explain which parts depend on real events.
Write full lines for the subjects to say, so the client feels sure of the result.
Scripted lines make real people sound stiff and turn the documentary into an advert.
Tell the client that documentaries cannot be planned, so they will simply have to trust you.
This worries clients and gives them nothing to approve or budget around.
Send the treatment from a past film and say yours will be much the same.
A past treatment doesn't say what this shoot will capture.
A02.why: A list of expected moments gives the client a shape to agree on, while leaving room for what really happens.

A02.q: Your film on India's 1983 cricket World Cup win needs old Doordarshan broadcast clips. When do you deal with the rights?
options: Contact the rights holder in pre-production to learn the cost, terms and time it will take.
Cut with clips from YouTube now, and clear the rights once the edit is locked.
If the clips turn out too costly or unavailable, you may have to rebuild whole sequences.
Skip clearance, since the clips are over forty years old and are widely shared online.
Age and popularity do not end ownership, and broadcasters will reject uncleared material.
Use extracts under ten seconds, since short extracts need no permission.
There is no safe length for broadcast clips.
A02.why: Asking at the start tells you if the footage is affordable and available before your story depends on it.

A02.q: A subject offers her late father's home movies from the 1970s for your film. Some clips have a Hindi film song playing in the background. What do you do?
options: Get written permission from whoever holds the rights, and check the song needs its own clearance.
Use the clips freely, since the family has handed you the tapes and is clearly happy for you to use them.
Having the tapes is not written permission, and it says nothing about the song.
Credit her father on screen, which covers your use of the home movies.
A credit is a courtesy, not permission, and the music rights remain uncleared.
Swap the song for new music and treat the home movies as cleared.
The home movies still need the rights holder's permission.
A02.why: Footage and music are owned separately, so both need clear, written permission before you use them.

A02.q: Your documentary's key scene is the evening aarti on the ghats, shot handheld in low light with live sound. How do you prepare?
options: Go on an earlier evening with the same camera and mic, shoot a few minutes, and review it.
Book the full crew for the main night and adjust your settings on the spot as the light changes.
If noise, focus or sound fail, you find out only when the real moment is gone.
Hire the biggest lights you can, so the low light is no longer a worry.
Big lights may not be allowed, can spoil the mood, and still leave sound untested.
Shoot the aarti on a phone the night before to check the light.
A phone doesn't show how your camera and mic will cope.
A02.why: A small trial with the real kit shows you the problems while there is still time to solve them.

A02.q: How does Deakins use a location scout?
options: To picture the shots in the real space and solve problems like light before shoot day.
To choose the best-looking place, and leave the lighting choices for the shoot day itself.
He treats lighting and other problems as things to solve during the scout, not later.
Mainly to check parking, power and permits for the crew and trucks.
Logistics matter, but he describes the scout as a creative planning step.
To choose where to put the lights once the crew arrives on the day.
Problems like light should be solved before shoot day.
A02.why: Seeing the shots in the actual place lets him spot problems and plan fixes before the main shoot.

A03.q: A jewellery shop owner in Surat asks you for "a few videos for Instagram" and wants a price today. What do you do before quoting?
options: List the number of videos, lengths, shoot days and rounds of changes, and get the owner to agree by email.
Give a round figure now and work out the number of videos together during the edit.
Without fixed numbers, the job can keep growing while your fee stays the same.
Agree the details on a phone call and start booking your crew straight away so you don't lose the job.
A phone call leaves no record, so both sides will remember the deal differently later.
Quote a price per video and say changes will be fixed whenever they come up.
No limit on changes lets the work grow without pay.
A03.why: A written list of what you will deliver and how many changes are included gives both sides one clear reference. Any request beyond it becomes a new, priced item.

A03.q: Halfway through editing a wedding film, the family asks for an extra reel and a third round of changes. Your signed document says one film and two rounds. What do you do?
options: Point to the signed document kindly, and offer the reel and extra round as a paid add-on with a new date.
Do both for free to keep the family happy, since happy clients bring more referrals and good reviews.
Free extras teach the client that the agreement doesn't matter, and your time goes unpaid.
Refuse both firmly and deliver only what is listed, with no further discussion.
A flat refusal harms the relationship when a paid option would serve both sides.
Do the extra reel for free but charge for the third round of changes.
Giving part away sets a pattern of free work.
A03.why: The signed document lets you say yes to extra work without arguing. You protect your time and the client still gets what they want.

A03.q: In Curren Sheldon's tutorial, why are budget assumptions written down before the costs are filled in?
options: So anyone can see what plan the numbers rest on, and what must change if that plan changes.
So the budget looks more detailed and professional when the client first opens the spreadsheet.
Assumptions are a working tool for decisions, not decoration for the client.
So you can skip detailed line items and just give a total for each department.
Assumptions explain the line items, they don't replace them.
So the client can negotiate each line of the budget separately.
Assumptions explain the plan; they aren't a negotiating tool.
A03.why: Assumptions like shoot days and crew size drive every number. When a plan shrinks, you change the assumptions and the costs follow.
A03.video: How To Make A Film Budget | Tutorial + Free Download

A03.q: A client asks you to cut your quote by 30%. Using the method from the budget tutorial, what is the best approach?
options: Build a smaller plan, such as fewer days or crew, budget it, and show both versions side by side.
Reduce every line in the existing budget by 30% and send the new total back.
Cutting numbers without changing the plan leaves you doing the same work for less money.
Keep the plan exactly as it is, and quietly remove the contingency line to hit the client's target.
Contingency is your cushion for surprises, and removing it only hides the real cost.
Offer to cut your day rate by 30% and keep the same plan.
You would do the same work for less pay.
A03.why: Comparing the original and reduced plans shows the client exactly what they lose for the saving. Then they can make an informed choice.
A03.video: How To Make A Film Budget | Tutorial + Free Download

A03.q: You are quoting a two-day factory shoot in Pune for a Mumbai client. Your sheet has crew fees and camera rental. What is most likely missing?
options: Travel, stay, meals and local transport for the crew and the gear.
A second set of lenses in case the client wants more variety.
Extra gear is a choice, while getting the crew there is a cost you cannot avoid.
A new editing software subscription for this one project.
Software is usually part of your general running costs, not a missing project line.
A line for the client's staff time spent in review meetings.
Travel and living costs are the usual missing items on out-of-town shoots.
A03.why: Out-of-town shoots carry real costs beyond fees and gear. Leaving them out eats directly into your profit.

A03.q: According to StudioBinder's guide, what makes a call sheet useful on the day?
options: Each person finds their call time, location details, key contacts and the day's plan in one place.
It lists every shot in detail so the camera team knows exactly what to frame.
That is the job of a shot list, while a call sheet coordinates people, times and places.
It replaces all other messages, so the crew never needs to be contacted again before the shoot day.
A call sheet is the main reference, but last checks with the crew are still needed.
It records what was filmed each day, for the editor to use later.
That describes a shot log, not a call sheet.
A03.why: A good call sheet answers where, when and who for everyone. That cuts down confusion and phone calls on the shoot day.
A03.video: A Producer's Guide to Call Sheets

A03.q: You booked a makeup artist and a drone operator for a product launch in Bengaluru. The client then moves the event by a week. What went wrong?
options: People were booked before the client had fixed the date with their venue and team.
The makeup artist and the drone operator should have been booked even earlier.
Booking earlier makes the problem worse if the date itself is not settled.
The call sheet was not sent early enough to the client for review.
The call sheet comes much later and cannot fix an unsettled date.
The vendors should have been warned that the date might change.
The mistake was booking before the date was fixed.
A03.why: Every booking depends on the date. Settle it first, then book people, then gear and venue.

A03.q: It is the evening before a shoot at a car showroom in Chennai. The call sheet went out last week. What do you do now?
options: Message each crew member and the showroom contact to check time, address and access, and wait for replies.
Trust that everyone read last week's call sheet carefully, and get some rest before tomorrow's early start.
Plans change in a week, and an unread message can leave you short of crew.
Post one reminder in the group chat and treat no reply as a yes.
Silence is not an answer, so you only find out who is missing on the day.
Call only the director and trust them to pass the details on.
Everyone must confirm for themselves.
A03.why: A personal check the day before catches changes while there is still time to fix them.

A03.q: In Caleb Pike's corporate video guide, why does a clear chain of command matter on the client side?
options: So feedback comes through one agreed contact, not from everyone who happens to be in the room.
So the video crew can overrule the client on any creative choice on set.
The point is clear decisions on both sides, not the crew taking over.
So the most senior executive can give their notes straight to the editor at any time they like.
Bypassing the agreed contact creates mixed messages and extra rework.
So the client can say who pays for each change.
A chain of command is about who gives feedback, not who pays.
A03.why: One route for decisions stops conflicting instructions. The crew knows whose word is final.

A03.q: Based on the guide's section on client notes, what do you do when several managers send different notes on the same cut?
options: Ask your main contact to merge them into one list and settle the clashes before you edit.
Apply each note in the order it arrived, so that nobody on the client's side feels ignored.
Clashing notes will undo each other and waste editing time.
Pick the notes you agree with creatively and leave the rest out.
It is not your call to decide between the client's own people.
Follow only the most senior manager's notes and ignore the rest.
Other managers' needs go unaddressed and can cause a dispute later.
A03.why: The client must resolve its own disagreements. You then edit once from a single, clear set of notes.

A03.q: On a shoot at a bank's office, a junior marketing staffer asks you to change the background, which goes against the approved brief. What do you do?
options: Note the request politely and check with the named decision-maker before changing anything.
Make the change right away, since anyone from the client side speaks for the client.
The approved brief may be overruled by someone without the authority to do so.
Smile, say yes, and carry on shooting exactly as you had planned.
Pretending to agree causes trouble later when they see nothing changed.
Refuse flatly because the request breaks the approved brief.
Refusing rudely harms the relationship; check with the decision-maker instead.
A03.why: Checking with the right person respects everyone. It also protects you from blame for changes nobody approved.

A03.q: You send a rough cut of a hotel brand film to the client in Jaipur. They reply only with notes on colour and title fonts. What do you do?
options: Save those notes for the fine cut, and ask them to confirm the story order and length in writing.
Fix the colour and fonts right away, since those are what the client noticed first.
Polishing now wastes time if the story order changes later.
Treat their reply as approval of the whole cut, and move straight on to the final delivery files.
Silence on structure is not agreement, and it can come back as a big change later.
Make the colour and font changes and ask them to look again in two weeks.
The story order is the thing to confirm first.
A03.why: A rough cut review is about structure, not polish. Getting the order and length agreed first means later notes stay small.

A03.q: At fine cut, the client wants to move the main interview to the start and reorder the whole story. They approved the rough cut in writing. What do you do?
options: Remind them the order was approved at rough cut, and quote the extra time and cost to re-cut it.
Quietly redo the whole structure for free so the project stays friendly.
This makes the earlier approval meaningless and costs you days of unpaid work.
Refuse the change and send the fine cut exactly as it is now.
A refusal with no option leaves an unhappy client when a paid change would work.
Re-order the film and quietly add the extra time to the delivery date, without telling them the reason.
Hidden extra work and delay damage trust.
A03.why: The written approval shows this is new work. Offering it at a cost keeps the relationship and your schedule fair.

A03.q: You are planning an outdoor shoot on a Kochi beach in late June. What is the best preparation?
options: Arrange a covered indoor option and agree a rain date with the client in advance.
Check the weather forecast on the morning of the shoot and decide what to do then.
By the morning it is too late to book a new place or move the crew.
Pack rain covers and umbrellas and shoot in whatever weather comes.
Covers protect gear, but heavy rain can still make the footage unusable.
Ask the client to cancel if it rains, and to pay a cancellation fee.
This doesn't protect the shoot; it only shifts the loss.
A03.why: June is monsoon season in Kerala. A ready second location and date mean rain changes the plan, not the outcome.

A03.q: You are the only camera operator at a one-time product launch that cannot be repeated. What do you pack as your safety net?
options: A spare camera body, extra charged batteries and cards, and a second audio recorder.
One camera with several extra lenses so you have more shot variety.
More lenses help creatively but do nothing if the camera body fails.
One camera, plus a firm promise to the client that you will reshoot if anything fails.
A live event cannot be reshot, so that promise cannot be kept.
A tripod and a wide lens, to cover the event from one position.
One angle can't protect against gear failure.
A03.why: For events that happen once, every key item needs a backup ready on the day. Spares turn a failure into a short pause.

A04.q: You have rented a new cinema lens for a wedding shoot next week. You have never used this model. What do you do?
options: Pick it up early, film a test scene at your planned settings, and check the clips on a big monitor.
Read reviews and watch sample footage online, then use it straight away on the wedding day.
Other people's footage won't show you how this copy works with your camera and settings.
Bring it to the venue and shoot a few quick frames before the guests start to arrive.
If you find a problem at the venue, there is no time left to fix it or swap the lens.
Test it on a quick walk around the rental shop, judging by the viewfinder only.
A viewfinder doesn't show how it behaves at your wedding settings.
A04.why: Problems like soft focus, flare or a bad mount show up in a calm test. Then you can fix them before the day that matters.

A04.q: A client's ad needs you to choose between two lenses. You will test both. How do you make the comparison fair?
options: Film the same scene, light and settings on both, and label every clip clearly as you go.
Film each lens on a different scene, so you can see how it handles many kinds of shots and light.
When the scene changes, you can't tell if a difference comes from the lens or the scene.
Film both lenses, then judge them on the camera's screen while you are still on set.
A small screen hides softness and colour shifts that will show up later on a big display.
Film the same scene on both, but with each lens at its own best aperture.
Different settings make the comparison unfair.
A04.why: Only one thing should change between clips: the lens. Clear labels stop you from mixing up the results when you compare them later.

A04.q: At an outdoor reception, the bride wears a white saree with gold work. You are filming her close up. How do you set your exposure?
options: Set exposure for her face, then use zebras (stripes over near-white areas) to check the saree.
Let auto exposure average the whole frame so the overall picture looks balanced on screen.
Auto exposure doesn't know the face matters most, and it often lets the bright saree burn out.
Make the image quite bright on purpose, then pull the saree back down in the edit later.
Once bright areas turn pure white, the detail is gone and no edit can bring it back.
Expose for the saree so the gold is perfect, then brighten her face in the grade.
Her face would be too dark to recover well.
A04.why: The face is what people look at, so it sets the exposure. Zebras warn you if the saree is about to turn pure white and lose its gold detail.

A04.q: In the In Depth Cine video, what trade-off do cinematographers weigh when they set exposure?
options: Detail in the bright areas against a well-exposed subject, measured with tools, not by eye.
How to keep the histogram centred in the middle so that every shot gets the same exposure.
A centred histogram ignores what matters in the frame, like a dark face or a bright sky.
How bright the image looks on the camera monitor, since that screen shows the final picture.
Monitor brightness can change, so pros rely on measuring tools like false colour instead.
Keep noise in the shadows lowest by exposing as bright as possible.
Brightest isn't best; bright areas lose detail.
A04.why: Exposure is a judgement about what to protect. Tools like false colour, which paints brightness levels in set colours, help measure that choice instead of guessing.

A04.q: You are filming a Kathak dancer at 25fps with the shutter at 1/50. Her hands look like smears when she spins. What do you change?
options: Set the shutter to around 1/250 or 1/500, then open the aperture or add light to keep brightness.
Switch to 50fps and keep the shutter at 1/50, then slow the clip down later in the edit.
Each frame is still exposed for 1/50 of a second, so the hands stay just as blurred.
Keep the same settings and add sharpening in the edit to bring back the detail in the hands.
Sharpening can't rebuild detail that motion blur has already smeared across the frame.
Raise the ISO and keep the shutter at 1/50 to keep the blur natural.
The blur stays; only a faster shutter sharpens her hands.
A04.why: A shorter shutter time freezes each frame more. Because less light comes in, you must make up for it with aperture, ISO or more light.

A04.q: You are filming a calm talking-head interview at 25fps under indoor lights in India. Which shutter speed do you choose?
options: Around 1/50, which gives natural motion and avoids flicker from the mains lights.
Around 1/1000, so every frame of the person talking is as sharp as it can possibly be.
Very short shutter times make normal movement look choppy and can cause light flicker.
Around 1/25, so more light reaches the sensor and you can keep the ISO nice and low.
Such a long shutter time makes even small head movements look smeared and soft.
Around 1/60, the standard setting for video everywhere.
1/60 can flicker under 50 Hz mains lights in India.
A04.why: About double the frame rate gives the motion blur our eyes expect. In India, mains power runs at 50Hz, so 1/50 also stays in step with the lights.

A04.q: You are interviewing a shop owner. A bright street doorway is right behind him, and you have no lights with you. What do you do?
options: Turn him so the doorway is off to one side and its light falls across his face.
Expose for his face and let the doorway behind him go fully white in the background.
A big white patch pulls the eye away from him and looks careless in a paid video.
Expose for the bright doorway and lift his dark face back up later in the edit.
Lifting deep shadows brings up grain and muddy colour on the most important part.
Move him into the shade of the room and leave the doorway directly behind him.
The doorway would still be much brighter than his face.
A04.why: Moving the subject or camera changes the contrast for free. The doorway turns from a problem behind him into soft light on his face.

A04.q: You are filming a haldi ceremony outdoors at noon. Harsh sun leaves half of each face in deep shadow. What is the best fix?
options: Move the group into open shade, or bounce light into the shadows with a reflector or white sheet.
Underexpose to save the bright skin, then lift the dark side of each face back up later in the grade.
Lifting dark shadows a lot adds grain and patchy colour to the skin.
Switch to auto exposure so the camera can keep adjusting as the faces move in and out.
Auto exposure keeps jumping between bright and dark, and it doesn't reduce the contrast at all.
Hold a phone torch on each face as people walk past.
A torch is too weak against noon sun.
A04.why: The camera can't hold both the sunlit and shadow side well. Softer light or filled shadows bring the range down so both sides keep detail.

A04.q: You are shooting a two-camera interview with a Sony and a Canon. Before you roll, what do you do so the shots match?
options: Set the same white balance in Kelvin, frame rate and shutter, then film a colour chart on both.
Put both cameras on auto white balance and fix any colour difference later in the edit.
Auto white balance can drift during the take, so each camera may change in a different way.
Look at each camera's screen and adjust the settings until the two pictures look the same.
Camera screens show colour differently, so matching by eye on them is not reliable.
Match the picture-profile names on both cameras and trust that they look the same.
Different brands read the same profile differently.
A04.why: Locked, matching settings remove most of the difference. The chart gives the colourist a shared reference to finish the match quickly.

A04.q: In Cullen Kelly's guide, why does he use colour space transforms (CSTs) on footage from different cameras?
options: To convert each camera's footage from its own colour space into one shared timeline space.
To add a creative film look to every clip so that they all share the same style.
A look is a creative step that comes later; CSTs handle the technical conversion first.
To make the footage from the cheaper camera sharper and closer to the main camera's quality.
CSTs change how colour and brightness are read, not the sharpness or detail of the image.
To reduce the file size so the timeline plays more smoothly.
A CST changes colour space, not file size.
A04.why: Each camera records colour in its own way. Bringing all of it into one working space means the same grade affects every camera the same way.
A04.video: The Pro Colorist Guide to Color Management in 2024

A04.q: A client wants web highlights from a three-day conference, delivered fast. Their budget for drives is small. How do you record?
options: Use an efficient 10-bit format at a medium bitrate, and work out the storage needed per day.
Record in RAW at the highest setting so the footage has the most quality you can get.
RAW fills drives fast and slows the edit, which this short, quick web job doesn't need.
Record at the lowest bitrate the camera offers so you save as much space as you can.
Very low bitrates break up in dim halls and fall apart when you colour correct the footage.
Record only proxies and discard the camera originals to save drive space.
Throwing away the originals removes your best quality.
A04.why: Bitrate is how much data the camera saves each second. The job needs clean, gradable footage, not maximum quality, and planning storage stops you running out on day two.

A04.q: The Adobe video on colour management explains why the editor must know how footage was recorded. What is the reason?
options: So the software reads the colour correctly and it shows right on the final screen, like web or TV.
Because it only matters when you deliver files for a cinema, not for web or TV videos.
Every output, including phones and web, needs the footage read and converted correctly.
Because a higher bitrate setting will fix any colour problems, as long as it is set right on export.
Bitrate controls how much data is saved, not whether the colour is read and shown correctly.
Because the editor has to tell the camera which settings to use.
The editor reads the footage; it can't change the camera.
A04.why: Colour management links three things: how it was recorded, the space you edit in, and where it will be watched. If one link is wrong, the colours shift.

A04.q: In the hybrid AI and live action video, what do you plan on set so the composite works?
options: Clean plates and reference objects, matching perspective and focus.
Nothing extra. The AI tools can fix it all in post.
Without plates and references, the composite looks fake.
Only the final performance, with the best take marked.
The compositor needs more than the take.
A wide shot of the whole scene, so the AI has more picture to work with.
A wide shot doesn't give the AI a clean plate or perspective data.
A04.why: Hybrid shots are made on set as much as in post.
A04.video: Hybrid AI and Live Action Filmmaking

A04.q: You plan to replace a plain wall with an AI-made bookshelf. What should you capture on set?
options: A clean plate of the wall, the lens details and the light direction.
Just the take with the actor, framed the way you want it.
The compositor needs references to match.
A photo of a real bookshelf for the AI to copy from.
Helpful, but the plate and camera details matter more.
A short video of the wall from several angles for the AI to learn from.
Angles of the wall aren't a clean plate for your shot.
A04.why: Capture what the compositor needs to match the shot.

A05.q: You are filming a testimonial for a family sweet shop. The owner freezes and his answers sound stiff. What do you do?
options: Ask him to pack a box of barfi for a regular customer while he talks.
Tell him to relax, smile more and just be himself on camera.
Asking for a feeling makes people watch themselves, so they get stiffer.
Show him playback of the stiff take so he can see the problem.
Seeing a bad take usually makes a nervous person more self-conscious.
Give him the key points on a card and ask him to read them straight to camera.
Reading makes him stiffer, not more natural.
A05.why: A familiar task with his hands takes his mind off the camera. His real warmth shows up on its own.

A05.q: At a wedding you have two minutes before the next ritual. You want an emotional shot of the bride with her grandmother. How do you direct it?
options: Ask the grandmother to fix the bride's dupatta and give her a blessing.
Ask them to hug and both look into the lens with a big smile.
Looking at the lens breaks the private moment, and the smile reads as posed.
Film them quietly from afar and hope a moment happens soon.
With only two minutes, hoping often gives you nothing usable.
Tell them to hold hands and look at each other lovingly for ten seconds.
It is posed; ask for an action, not an expression.
A05.why: A real gesture between them creates real feeling. The emotion comes from what they do, not from posing.

A05.q: On a corporate shoot, the CEO will walk into the office and greet staff. Your gaffer (lighting lead) wants to lay the track and set lights right away. What do you do first?
options: Have someone walk the route and mark where the CEO stops and turns.
Lay the track now and ask the CEO to follow its line later.
Forcing a person to fit the gear makes the walk look stiff and unnatural.
Skip the walkthrough and shoot the first walk as a real take.
An unplanned take usually misses marks and costs more takes than it saves.
Rehearse the walk with the CEO first, and mark his positions after the lights are set.
Track and lights depend on where he stops, so mark the route first.
A05.why: Once you know the real path and stops, you can put the camera, track and lights where they actually help. Doing it the other way means moving everything twice.

A05.q: In the StudioBinder blocking example, what does rehearsing the movement give the crew?
options: A clear plan, so the actors and the camera move together.
A chance to perfect the actors' emotions before the shoot.
The example is about planning movement and position, not performance feeling.
Time to test the lens look and colour grade early on.
Look tests are useful, but that is not what blocking rehearsal is for.
A timing check, to learn how long the scene will run in the final edit.
Blocking rehearses movement, not the final timing.
A05.why: Blocking rehearsal works out who moves where and when. Then the camera can be planned around that coordinated action.
A05.video: Cinematic Film Composition — Blocking, Staging & Composition

A05.q: A shy pharmacy owner rushes through her lines on take two. The client is watching. What do you say?
options: "That was warm, I liked it. This time, pause after the shop name."
"Okay. Slow down, smile more, and look up at the end too."
Three notes at once overload a nervous person and none of them stick.
"That was great! Let's just go again and make it even better."
Kind, but she still has no idea what to change, so the next take repeats the problem.
"Don't rush. You're speaking too fast, so slow right down."
A negative note makes a shy person tighter.
A05.why: Kind words first lower her guard. One clear, specific note is easy to act on, so the next take improves.

A05.q: In Caleb Pike's corporate video guide, what helps most when the talent is shy and not a trained presenter?
options: Chatting casually before rolling and keeping the set calm.
Bringing in more crew so the set feels more professional.
More people watching makes a shy person more nervous, not less.
Handing them a full script to learn word for word.
Memorising lines adds pressure, and non-actors tend to sound robotic.
Giving her a long list of notes to remember before the next take.
Too many notes overwhelm someone who isn't used to the camera.
A05.why: Shy people relax when it feels like a conversation, not a performance. A calm, friendly set gets more natural answers.

A05.q: You are shooting a doctor's interview alone, with the camera on a tripod. Where do you place yourself to ask the questions?
options: Sit right beside the lens, at the doctor's eye height.
Sit across the room so you can watch the whole frame.
Her eyes will drift far from the lens and she will look disconnected.
Stand behind the camera so she looks over the top of it.
She will look upward, which reads oddly and shows the whites of her eyes.
Sit beside the lens but a little higher than her, so she looks up at you.
Looking up changes how she appears; match her eye height.
A05.why: Sitting close to the lens keeps her gaze just off camera. It looks natural and connected to the viewer.

A05.q: Based on the StudioBinder blocking tutorial, you want one person in a two-person scene to feel more powerful. Which staging choice helps?
options: Place them closer to camera or higher, with the other further back.
Keep both side by side and add music to show who leads.
Music can help, but the blocking itself then tells no story.
Frame both the same size in the centre to stay balanced.
Equal framing makes the two people feel equal, which is the opposite goal.
Frame the powerful person from slightly above, looking down at the other.
Looking down on someone makes them look weaker, not stronger.
A05.why: Where people stand and how the camera sees them shows status. Size, height and depth in frame do the storytelling.

A05.q: You have two cameras for a sangeet dance performance on stage. How do you set them up?
options: One wide on the whole stage, one tight following the lead dancer.
One wide on the stage, one on the audience the whole time.
Crowd shots are nice, but you have no backup angle of the dance itself.
Both medium from the front, side by side, with the same lens.
Matching frames give the editor nothing new to cut to.
One wide on the stage, one tight on the drummer at the back.
The lead dancer is the focus, not the drummer.
A05.why: A wide and a tight shot of the same dance show different things. The editor can cut between them freely and hide mistakes.

A05.q: A startup wants a podcast with two hosts. You have three cameras. How do you use them?
options: A wide of both hosts, plus a close single on each host.
All three on the wide from slightly different angles.
Three near-identical wides cut together badly and miss faces.
Two on the main host and one wide, since he talks most.
The second host's reactions get no clean shot to cut to.
One wide of both hosts and two on the guest who speaks the most.
Both hosts need coverage, and the wide shot is the safety.
A05.why: Each camera covers something the others cannot. You can always cut to whoever speaks or reacts.

A05.q: On a brand shoot for a handloom saree business, a power cut costs two hours. You can only finish three of the eight shots left. What do you keep?
options: The weaver's hands at the loom and the founder's main line.
The drone shot of the village you planned as the opener.
It looks great, but the film still works without it.
A second take of the product shot you already got well.
You already have a good take, so this adds very little.
A product still of every saree in the range.
With limited time, the story and the weaver matter more.
A05.why: Shots that carry the story come first. Style shots and safety takes go when time runs out.

A05.q: You have one day to film a promo for a small restaurant, built around the chef telling his story. Which shot do you schedule first?
options: The chef's interview, since the whole film hangs on it.
The dish close-ups, while the window light is still soft.
Pretty food shots can be grabbed later, but no interview means no film.
The outside of the restaurant, since it is quick to get.
Easy shots feel productive, but they can be dropped if the day runs late.
The chef's walk to the market, since it adds context.
The interview is the core; filming it first protects the film.
A05.why: Putting the story's backbone first protects it if the day slips. Everything else can be cut or rushed without ruining the film.

A06.q: A wedding planner wants a warm, friendly testimonial for her website. Your key light leaves one side of her face in deep shadow. What do you change?
options: Bounce light into the shadow side so it sits closer to the bright side
Add a strong backlight behind her so she stands out from the wall
A backlight separates her from the background but leaves the heavy face shadow as it is.
Leave it and lift the shadow side later in colour correction
Lifting deep shadows in the edit adds noise and often looks flat and muddy.
Raise the key light higher and point it more steeply down.
A steeper angle deepens the eye shadows.
A06.why: A smaller gap between the bright and dark sides of the face feels open and gentle. Bouncing light into the shadow side does this on set, where it looks cleanest.

A06.q: In Mark Bone's interview system, why does he stress-test and document the setup at the end?
options: So he can trust it holds up and rebuild or match it on another day
So the client can sign off on the lighting before the shoot
His steps are about his own reliability, not getting client approval.
So the guest gets used to the bright lights before the filming starts
Helping the guest relax is useful, but it is not why he checks and records the setup.
So the footage can be graded faster in the edit.
He documents it so the look can be rebuilt, not for grading.
A06.why: Checking the setup under real conditions catches problems early. Notes and photos let him match the same look later, for another interview or a reshoot.
A06.video: How I Light Every Interview (my 10-step system)

A06.q: You are filming a night scene in a Chennai home. A table lamp sits beside the actor in the frame. Where do you place your key light?
options: On the lamp's side, at a similar height and warm colour
Straight in front of the actor so the face is fully lit
Light from the front does not match the lamp, so the scene looks fake.
Behind the actor on the far side as a strong rim light
A rim from the far side has no reason to be there if the lamp is beside them.
Opposite the lamp, at the same height, to light the other side of the actor.
The lamp should explain the light; the opposite side doesn't.
A06.why: Viewers believe light that seems to come from the lamp they can see. Matching its side, height and colour sells the scene.

A06.q: In the Aputure continuity demo, what must stay the same when cutting from the wide shot to the reverse angles (shots from the opposite side)?
options: The direction the key light seems to come from in the scene
The exact physical position of every light on set
Lights often move for close-ups; what matters is how the light reads on screen.
The brightness of each light, with no changes at all for the close-ups
The demo shows close-ups can be adjusted in strength while staying consistent.
The size of the light source, whichever lens is used.
The direction of the light is what should match; size can change.
A06.why: If the key flips sides between shots, the cut feels wrong. You can move and tweak lights for each angle as long as the light still seems to come from the same place.

A06.q: You are filming an interview in an office with big windows and warm ceiling bulbs. You have one bicolour LED panel (it can switch between warm and cool). What do you do?
options: Switch off the bulbs and set the LED and camera to match the daylight
Set the camera to auto white balance so it sorts out the colours
Auto cannot fix two colours on one face and may shift during the take.
Set the camera halfway between warm and cool, and keep all the lights on
A middle setting still leaves one side blue and the other orange.
Keep the bulbs on and set the LED to warm to match them.
Mixed daylight and bulbs makes the colours clash.
A06.why: Window light is the strongest source and the hardest to change, so build around it. Removing or matching the other sources gives one clean colour on the face.

A06.q: At an evening sangeet, the stage lights are warm orange. Your on-camera LED is set to daylight and faces look blue next to the stage. What is the best fix?
options: Warm your LED with an orange gel (coloured filter) to match the stage
Set the camera white balance to daylight to keep the LED neutral
Then the whole stage turns very orange and the mix is still there.
Keep shooting and fix the two colours separately in the edit
Separating mixed colours on moving faces in the edit is slow and rarely clean.
Turn the LED off and rely on the stage lights alone, whatever the faces look like.
Faces may be too dark to read.
A06.why: Matching your light to the room's light means one white balance setting works for everything. A gel or the warm setting on a bicolour light does this quickly.

A06.q: You are lighting an interview in a small room with white walls. The shadow side of the face looks flat because the walls bounce light back. What do you do?
options: Hang a black cloth close on the shadow side to soak up the bounce
Turn up the key light so the bright side stands out more
The walls bounce the extra light too, so the face stays flat.
Add a second soft light on the shadow side to even it out
More light on the shadow side makes the face even flatter.
Move the key light further away to soften its effect on the walls.
Distance doesn't remove the bounce that flattens the shadow side.
A06.why: Black cloth absorbs light instead of reflecting it. Taking light away from the shadow side brings back shape in a bright room.

A06.q: You are filming a bride at an outdoor haldi at noon. Harsh sun leaves hard shadows under her eyes. You have a small crew. What helps most?
options: Hold a thin white diffusion cloth above her to spread the sunlight
Point a strong LED straight at her face to fill in the shadows under her eyes
A small LED cannot compete with noon sun and adds glare in her eyes.
Close the aperture a lot so the shadows look less dark
Changing exposure does not change how hard the shadows fall.
Move her under a tree and rely on the dappled light.
Dappled light makes patchy light on her face.
A06.why: A diffusion cloth turns a small hard source like the sun into a large soft one. The shadows become gentle without fighting the sun.

A06.q: You are interviewing a professor who wears glasses. Your soft key light shows up as a bright patch in his lenses. Which move usually fixes it?
options: Raise the key and angle it down so the reflection bounces away
Move the key closer to the camera so it sits behind the lens
Light near the camera reflects almost straight back into the lens.
Keep the key where it is and turn its brightness down a lot
A dimmer light still shows a patch and leaves the face underlit.
Switch to a smaller, harder light so the reflection becomes smaller.
A harder light still reflects in the lenses.
A06.why: Light bounces off glass at the same angle it hits. Raising and angling the key sends the reflection down and out of the camera's view.

A06.q: In the Aputure product video, why does the size and shape of the light matter so much for a glossy bottle?
options: The light itself shows up as the highlight on the bottle's surface
Bigger lights make the label colours look brighter
The point is what the shiny surface reflects, not label brightness.
A small hard light is needed to make the glass look sharp
A small hard source gives a tiny harsh spot, not a clean highlight.
The size of the light doesn't matter; only the label colours decide the look.
The size of the light decides what the highlight looks like.
A06.why: A shiny surface acts like a mirror, so the viewer sees the shape of the source. Choosing that shape and moving the light or camera controls how the highlight looks.

A06.q: You are filming a sweet shop owner in a busy Mumbai market lane. Your light stand is on the pavement and people keep walking past. What do you do first?
options: Weigh the stand with a sandbag and tape or cover every cable
Raise the light higher so people can walk under it
A taller stand with no weight tips over more easily in a crowd.
Shoot quickly, and ask people walking past to be careful around the gear
Busy passers-by will not notice, and one trip can hurt someone.
Move the stand to the road so it is clear of the pavement.
The road is more dangerous for people and the stand.
A06.why: Weight keeps a stand from falling if it is bumped. Taped or covered cables stop people tripping on a crowded pavement.

A06.q: At a family function in an old house, you plug three lights into one extension board. The power keeps tripping. What is the right move?
options: Spread the lights across separate circuits and check what each can handle
Keep resetting the switch and finish the shoot quickly
Repeated tripping is a warning of overload and can cause heat or fire.
Use a bigger extension board so all the lights fit on one plug safely
More sockets do not add capacity, so the wall circuit is still overloaded.
Run the lights at half power so the board stops tripping.
The overload remains; spread the load across circuits.
A06.why: Each wall circuit can only carry so much power. Spreading the load stops trips and keeps old wiring from overheating.

A07.q: Two actors walk and talk around a small kitchen in medium shots. Both wear silk kurtas that rustle when they move. Which mic setup gives you the cleanest dialogue?
options: A boom held above them, just out of frame, following each line
A lav taped under each kurta, close to the chest
Silk rubbing on a hidden lav creates rustle that is very hard to remove later.
A shotgun mic mounted on top of the camera
The camera follows the frame, not the voice, so the mic is often too far and off target.
A lav on one actor, and a shotgun mic on the camera for the other.
The two voices would sound different, and the lav rustles on silk.
A07.why: A boom stays close to the mouths without touching the clothes, and it can follow the actors as they move. It is the usual choice for scripted scenes with movement.

A07.q: In Curtis Judd's comparisons, which change cut down the harsh "s" sounds in speech?
options: Aiming the mic a little off the mouth instead of straight at it
Pointing the mic straight at the mouth, from a little closer up than before
Aiming dead on at the mouth makes the sharp "s" sounds stronger, not softer.
Taking the foam cover off the mic for a cleaner tone
Removing the foam does not solve sibilance and leaves the mic open to breath pops.
Moving the mic further away so it hears the whole room.
Further away means more echo and less clarity.
A07.why: Sibilance, the hissy "s" sound, is strongest right in front of the mouth. Small changes in angle and height move the mic out of that path while keeping the voice full.

A07.q: You are filming a podcast for a Pune startup with three guests at one table. One guest laughs loudly and often talks over the others. Which setup lets you fix this best in the edit?
options: A lav on each guest, each recorded to a separate channel
Two lavs mixed together onto one channel to save space
Once voices share one channel, you cannot lower one person without lowering the other.
One shotgun mic on a stand in the middle of the table
One mic picks up the loud guest strongly and the quiet ones weakly, with no way to rebalance them.
One omnidirectional mic on a stand in the centre of the table.
One mic can't separate the guests' voices.
A07.why: When every voice lives on its own channel, you can turn down the loud guest and lift the quiet ones without touching anyone else.

A07.q: In the edit, you hear a faint hollow echo whenever one guest speaks, because the other guests' lavs also pick up that voice. What do you do?
options: Lower or mute the channels of guests who are not speaking then
Keep every channel at full level so no word is ever missed
Leaving all mics open is exactly what makes the same voice arrive twice and sound hollow.
Add a little reverb to all channels to blend the echo away
Reverb adds more space to the sound and makes the hollow effect worse, not better.
Pan each guest's channel to a different side.
Panning doesn't remove the picked-up voices.
A07.why: Each lav hears the speaker a fraction of a second apart, which causes phasing, a hollow sound. Bringing down the unused channels leaves one clean copy of the voice.

A07.q: You are filming a couple's pre-wedding interview on a mirrorless camera. The camera's audio input adds a lot of hiss. The client wants clean sound. What is your setup?
options: Run the mic into a dedicated recorder and keep scratch sound on the camera
Plug the mic into the camera and turn the input gain up high
Raising the camera's gain raises its hiss too, so the voice is louder but still noisy.
Use the dedicated recorder and switch the camera's audio off fully
Without any camera sound, you lose an easy guide for matching the files in the edit.
Plug the mic into both the recorder and the camera, and use the camera's sound in the edit.
The camera audio is the hissy one; keep the recorder as the main sound.
A07.why: A dedicated recorder usually has cleaner preamps, the circuits that boost the mic signal. The camera's scratch track gives you a reference and a second copy.

A07.q: Halfway through a CEO interview, you notice the camera's audio crackles from a loose cable. The recorder's levels look clean. What do you do?
options: Confirm the recorder files are fine, then fix the cable at the next natural pause
Stop the CEO mid-answer and restart the whole interview from the very top
The clean recorder already has the answer, so stopping wastes the client's limited time.
Ignore it for now, and leave both recordings unchecked until you get to the edit later
If the recorder also had a problem, you would only find out when it is too late to fix.
Re-seat the cable while the CEO is still speaking.
Handling the cable mid-answer creates more noise.
A07.why: Because the recorder holds the main sound, the camera problem is not an emergency. You check your main copy and repair the backup when it will not interrupt.

A07.q: During a documentary shoot, a take starts before anyone marks it. The moment is real and you cannot stop it. How do you help the editor match picture and sound?
options: Mark the end of the take instead, holding the slate upside down
Leave it unmarked and trust the editor to line up waveforms
Waveform matching can fail with noisy audio, so a mark is still the safer choice.
Stop the action and ask everyone to start the moment again
In documentary work you would lose a real moment that may never happen again.
Slate at the start of the next take and assume the editor can find this one.
The editor needs a marker for this take too.
A07.why: A tail slate, a mark at the end, works just as well for syncing. Holding it upside down tells the editor the mark is at the end, not the start.

A07.q: In the Deity video, all cameras and the recorder share timecode. Why does the crew still use a slate?
options: As a fallback in case a device drifts or loses its timecode
Because editing software cannot read timecode from audio files
Editing software reads timecode from audio files easily, so that is not the reason.
Because timecode only works on cameras and never on recorders
Timecode is designed to link cameras and recorders, which is the whole point of the video.
Because the slate stores the metadata for the recorder's files.
A slate gives a visible and audible marker, not metadata.
A07.why: Timecode can slip if a device is reset or its battery runs out. A visible mark gives a second way to sync if that happens.

A07.q: At the end of the production example in the Deity video, what is the main purpose of the sound report handed over with the files?
options: To show which files and takes go together, and note any problems
To prove to the client how many hours the sound crew worked
The report is a technical guide for the edit, not a timesheet.
To list the brand and model of every mic used on the day
Gear details may appear, but the key job is to explain files, takes and issues.
To explain how the sound was mixed for the final film.
A sound report is about the files, not the mix.
A07.why: A good report saves the editor hours of guessing. It links takes to files and flags anything that went wrong on set.

A07.q: You record a stand-up comedian at a small Bengaluru venue. You split one mic to both channels of a 24-bit recorder. How far below the main channel do you set the second one?
options: About 6 to 10 dB lower, so it stays clean but still usable
About 1 dB lower, so both channels match each other closely
A peak loud enough to distort the main channel will almost surely distort this one too.
About 30 dB lower, so nothing on stage could ever distort it
It is so quiet that boosting it later brings up heavy hiss and makes it hard to use.
About 15 dB lower, so it never matches the main channel.
Too low and it will be noisy when you need it.
A07.why: A gap of around 6 to 10 dB catches sudden laughs and shouts that clip the main channel, while staying loud enough to match it cleanly when you swap it in.

A07.q: In the edit of a 40 minute set, the main channel distorts on one loud shout at the 12 minute mark. You have a lower safety channel. What do you do?
options: Replace just that shout from the safety channel and match its level
Replace the whole set with the safety channel to be safe
Boosting the quieter channel for 40 minutes adds hiss everywhere when only one moment needed fixing.
Mix the safety channel in under the main one for the whole set
The distorted shout is still there in the main channel, so you will still hear it.
Lower the main channel for the whole set, to remove the distortion there.
That makes the whole set quieter and noisier.
A07.why: Clipping, when the sound goes over the maximum level, cannot be undone. Swapping only the damaged moment with the clean copy fixes it and keeps the rest at its best.

A07.q: You finish a dialogue scene in a Jaipur haveli. A ceiling fan ran during every take and street noise came through the window. What do you record before moving on?
options: A minute of the room in silence, with the fan and window as in the takes
A minute of the room in silence, with the fan off for cleaner sound
It will not match the takes, so the gaps in the edit will sound different from the dialogue.
Nothing extra, since the editor can always add a library ambience track later
A library track will not match this room's exact hum and street sound.
A minute of the room with the fan on but the window closed.
The room tone must match the takes, including the window.
A07.why: Room tone must sound exactly like the background of the takes. The editor uses it to fill gaps and smooth cuts without the sound changing.

A07.q: In the StudioBinder interior section, a nearly empty room with bare walls makes voices sound hollow. What is the suggested fix?
options: Add blankets or soft furnishings to soak up sound bouncing off walls
Raise the recorder gain, so the voice is clearly louder than the room's echo
Raising gain raises the echo too, so the room still sounds hollow.
Move the mic further back so it hears the whole room evenly
Moving the mic away picks up even more echo compared to the voice.
Hang the mic from a boom above the speakers' heads.
A boom doesn't fix the echo of bare walls.
A07.why: Hard walls reflect sound back into the mic. Soft materials absorb those reflections, so the voice sounds closer and cleaner.
A07.video: Recording Sound for Film — How to Get Pristine Audio

A07.q: In the StudioBinder exterior section, what is the main protection against wind noise outdoors?
options: A furry windshield over the mic, often called a dead cat
The thin foam cover that comes in the box with the mic itself
Basic foam works indoors but is usually not enough for real outdoor wind.
A low-cut filter added later in the edit to remove it
A filter can reduce some rumble, but strong wind bursts recorded on set cannot be fully removed.
Lower the recording gain when the wind rises.
Lower gain doesn't stop the wind rumble hitting the mic.
A07.why: The furry cover slows the wind before it hits the mic. Stopping wind noise at the source is far better than trying to fix it later.
A07.video: Recording Sound for Film — How to Get Pristine Audio

A08.q: After a wedding shoot in Lucknow, you copy six camera cards to your edit drive. The couple's family wants the cards back tonight. What do you do before formatting them?
options: Run checksum software that compares every card file with its copy
Open a few clips from each card and scrub through them
A spot check can miss a damaged or missing file that you never opened.
Confirm that the folder size on the drive matches the card
Two folders can be the same size and still hold a corrupted file.
Check the file count and total size against the card, then spot-play three clips.
Matching size and a few clips don't prove every file is intact.
A08.why: A checksum is a short code worked out from a file's data. If the codes match, the copy is identical, so the card is safe to wipe.

A08.q: You hand a client a drive of raw footage from a factory shoot. Weeks later they say some clips are broken. What would have protected you?
options: Sending a checksum list with the drive so they could test it on arrival
Sending a screenshot of the folder showing all the file names and their sizes
A list of names does not prove the data inside each file was intact.
Asking them to play every clip once when the drive arrived
Playing clips is slow and still misses small errors in the data.
A written note saying which clips you checked on your side.
A note doesn't let the client prove the files are intact.
A08.why: A checksum list lets both sides prove the files arrived exactly as they left, so you can show where any damage happened.

A08.q: You filmed an interview on a phone with a survivor of abuse, inside her home in Pune. The NGO will post it publicly. What do you do with the file?
options: Strip GPS and device details from the public copy, and archive the untouched original
Blur her face in the edit and upload the original file as it is
The file can still carry the GPS position of her home, which can expose her.
Wipe all hidden data from every copy, including your own archive
You lose the date, place and device details that may later prove the footage is real.
Upload the original with all its metadata to the NGO, and ask them to remove it.
Removing it later risks it being posted publicly with location data.
A08.why: The public file should not reveal where she lives. Your untouched archive keeps the full record in case the footage must be verified later.

A08.q: According to the WITNESS video, why does metadata matter when you hand footage to a lawyer or a news desk?
options: It helps them confirm when, where and on what device it was recorded
It keeps the picture quality high when the clip is shared onward
Metadata is information about the file, not the image quality itself.
It is mainly useful for sorting clips into bins inside an editor
Sorting is a small use, and the video stresses proving the source of footage.
It tells the editing software which colour profile to use.
That is a colour setting, not why a lawyer needs metadata.
A08.why: Metadata is data stored inside the file, like time, date and location. It helps others check that the footage is genuine and trace its source.

A08.q: A small Jaipur studio edits from one SSD and backs up to a second SSD kept in the same desk drawer. What single change protects them most?
options: Add a cloud copy or a drive kept at someone's home
Buy a third SSD and keep it in the same drawer
A fire, flood or theft at the studio would still take every copy at once.
Make a second folder copy on the editing SSD itself
If that one drive fails, both folders are lost together.
Label the second SSD clearly and keep it in a different drawer of the same desk.
A fire or theft still takes both.
A08.why: Copies in one building share the same risks. A copy in another place survives a fire, theft or water damage at the studio.

A08.q: Your two backups are identical hard drives from the same shop, bought on the same day. Why is this risky?
options: Drives from one batch can fail around the same time, so mix in cloud or another type
Identical drives copy more slowly, so the nightly backup will take far too long each night
Matching drives do not slow copying, and the real worry is failing together.
Identical drives confuse the computer, so files may save to the wrong one
Computers tell drives apart by name, so this is not the real danger.
Identical drives are slower because they share one controller.
Failure at the same time is the risk, not speed.
A08.why: Same model, same batch and same age means the same weak points. Using a different type, like cloud or tape, spreads the risk.

A08.q: You are cutting 6K footage from a corporate shoot on a laptop. Playback stutters and the deadline is in two days. What is the best approach?
options: Edit on low-resolution stand-ins, then switch to full files for grading and export
Convert the camera files to small files and delete the originals to save space
You lose the full-quality footage you need for the final grade and export.
Edit on low-resolution stand-ins and export the final straight from them
The client would get a soft, low-quality film instead of the 6K quality you shot.
Reduce the timeline's preview quality and leave the files as they are.
It may still stutter with 6K files; proxies are the fix.
A08.why: Small edit files keep playback smooth. Switching back to the camera files at the end gives full quality in the finished film.

A08.q: In Adobe's Premiere demo, why do proxies make teamwork easier?
options: Small files move easily between editors, and the edit can still swap back to camera files
They replace the camera files, so the team has much less footage to archive at the end
Proxies are temporary stand-ins and never replace the originals.
Each editor rebuilds the timeline on their own proxies before sharing
The same timeline works with proxies or full files, so no rebuild is needed.
They let editors skip colour and sound work later on.
Proxies are a working copy; the work continues on the originals.
