A08.why: Proxies are light enough to share and play on any machine. Premiere can toggle back to full-quality media whenever it is needed.

A08.q: Two camera operators and three editors will work on a three-day shoot for a jewellery brand. When should the file names be agreed?
options: Before the shoot, in a short written guide shared with everyone
After the shoot, when an assistant renames everything in one go for the editors
Renaming later is slow, causes errors and can break links in early edits.
Never formally, since each person can explain their own names
People forget, leave or fall sick, and then nobody can read the files.
During the shoot, with each operator choosing their own system.
Different systems clash when files merge.
A08.why: A rule agreed early means files are named right from the first card. Everyone can find anything without asking.

A08.q: Your team puts the shoot date at the start of every file name. Which format should you pick?
options: 20240315, with year, month, then day
15-03-24, with day, month, then year
Files sort by day first, so 2 April would land before 15 March.
15Mar2024, with the month as a short word
Files sort by day first, and month words sort alphabetically, so the order breaks.
March15 2024, with the month first and then the day.
It doesn't sort by date.
A08.why: Year, month, day sorts in true time order on every computer, so files line up correctly in any folder.

A08.q: A freelancer sends you a Premiere project and a drive of media. When you open it, every clip shows as offline. What do you do first?
options: Use Link Media, find one clip on the drive and let it locate the rest
Import all the clips again and rebuild the timeline from scratch
You throw away the freelancer's cuts and waste hours redoing their work.
Replace each offline clip by hand, one at a time, from the drive
This is slow and easy to get wrong when the folders are already in order.
Copy the media to your own drive and make a fresh project with the same name.
A fresh project loses the edit.
A08.why: When the folder structure is kept, pointing to one file lets Premiere find the others in the same place.

A08.q: Karl Soule's setup advice suggests testing a project before you hand it over. What is a good test?
options: Move the project and media to another drive and open it there
Save the project twice so there is a spare copy on your desktop
A spare project file does not show whether media links survive a move.
Trust that the project file stores the clips inside itself
A project only points to media files and does not contain them.
Send the project file alone and let the recipient find the media.
The recipient will have offline clips.
A08.why: Opening the moved project shows if any clip goes offline. You fix problems before the next person finds them.

A08.q: A client says, "Go back to the music we had two cuts ago." What makes this a quick fix?
options: Each saved cut has a number and a short note of what was edited
Each saved cut is named by its mood, like final, final_new, final_ok
Names like these do not show order, so nobody knows which was two cuts ago.
Only the latest cut is kept, so the drive stays tidy
The older cut with the music the client wants is gone.
Each cut is saved as a screen recording so you can scroll back to it.
A recording isn't an editable project.
A08.why: Numbers show the order of cuts, and the notes show where the music changed. You can open the right file in seconds.

A08.q: In Adobe's Productions video, what problem does this workflow mainly solve?
options: It lets editors share linked projects and locks any project in use
It suggests a story structure for long films so editors cut faster
Productions handles how projects are shared, not the story of the film.
It merges two editors' changes to one timeline automatically
It avoids clashes by locking projects, not by merging edits together.
It converts all project files to one format for each editor to read.
It links projects; it doesn't convert them.
A08.why: Splitting a big job into linked projects with locking stops two people overwriting each other's work.

A08.q: In the Magic Mask video, how do you avoid re-tracking masks after timeline changes?
options: Render the mattes and reuse them, with clear filenames and versions.
Re-track every time something changes.
That wastes hours.
Keep only the final export.
You lose the chance to change the grade later.
Track the mask again, but only on the shots that you changed in the edit.
Rendered mattes avoid re-tracking altogether.
A08.why: Rendered, named mattes save time in every revision.
A08.video: Never Retrack Magic Mask 2 in Resolve

A08.q: You hand a project to another editor. What should go with the AI mattes?
options: Source shots, rendered mattes, and names with shot and version.
Only the final exported video, so the files you hand over stay small.
They can’t make changes without the sources.
The mattes in one folder, without renaming them.
They won’t know which matte belongs to which shot.
Only the project file, as it holds the mattes inside it.
Rendered mattes are separate files and must travel with the project.
A08.why: A good handover can be picked up without asking you.

A09.q: You are cutting an 8-minute wedding film from a Lucknow shaadi. Your first cut runs from haldi to vidaai in the order things happened, and it feels flat. What do you try first?
options: Open on the father's emotional toast, then go back and build toward the pheras.
Keep the real order but trim every clip so the film moves faster.
Shorter clips change speed, but the film still has no shape or hook.
Put the best moments together in the first two minutes to grab attention.
Spending all your strongest moments early leaves nothing to build toward.
Keep the real order and add a voiceover from the groom to carry the story.
A voiceover doesn't fix a structure that feels flat.
A09.why: Moving a strong moment to the front gives the viewer a reason to watch. Arranging the rest to rise toward the pheras gives the film a shape that real time alone does not.

A09.q: In the pacing framework from Inside The Edit, what is the main job of thinking about pacing?
options: Planning how energy rises and falls across the whole film.
Making each clip as short as it can be without losing sense.
The video treats pacing as a whole-film shape, not just trimming single clips.
Keeping every scene at one steady speed so nothing feels jarring.
An even speed throughout flattens the film, which is the opposite of an arc.
Match every cut to the beat of the music.
Cutting on the beat sets rhythm but doesn't plan the energy across the film.
A09.why: The video shows pacing as an arc over the full piece. The worked scene comparisons show how fast and slow sections work together.
A09.video: Pacing in Film Editing — The Framework Pro Editors Use

A09.q: For a 12-minute documentary about a Varanasi weaver, his interview opens with many facts at once: family history, the loom's age, his debts, and that the loom will be sold next month. The buyers' visit comes at minute 9. How do you use these facts?
options: Spread them through the film, placing the sale news shortly before the buyers' visit.
Keep them together at the start, in the order he said them, to stay true to him.
So many facts at once are hard to hold, and the sale news fades before the visit.
Hold all of them back and reveal them together after the buyers have left.
Without the sale news, viewers watch the visit without knowing why it matters.
Cut everything except the sale news so the film stays simple.
Removing the other facts takes away what builds the stakes.
A09.why: Viewers can only hold a few facts at a time. Spacing them out, with the sale news just before the visit, turns an ordinary scene into a tense one.

A09.q: In the postproduction chapters of Roger Ross Williams's Sundance Collab session, how is the story shaped?
options: It is found and reshaped through working cuts, with the editor as a creative partner.
It is fixed in a script before shooting, and the editor follows that plan closely.
The session shows documentary story being discovered in the edit, not locked in advance.
The director cuts alone and brings in an editor only for the final polish.
The session stresses close teamwork with the editor during structure, not only at the end.
It is fixed in the first cut, and later cuts only trim for length.
Working cuts reshape the story, not just its length.
A09.why: In documentary, the real story often only appears in the edit room. Testing working cuts with an editor is how the order of facts and characters gets decided.
A09.video: Documentary: Finding and Shaping Your Story

A09.q: For a sweet shop's brand film, the owner recorded her story eight times. Take 3 is word-perfect but sounds rehearsed. In take 7 her voice catches and she pauses while talking about her late father, who started the shop. Which do you use?
options: Take 7, using a cutaway to cover the stumble if needed.
Take 3, because a business film should sound clean and confident.
A polished but rehearsed take can leave viewers unmoved, which defeats the purpose.
Join the best lines from several takes into one clean answer.
Stitching takes often breaks the voice and loses the feeling that made take 7 work.
Use Take 3 for the sound, laid over the pictures from Take 7.
The catch in her voice is the point; mixing takes loses it.
A09.why: Viewers connect with honest emotion more than with perfect wording. A cutaway (a short shot of something else) can hide a small stumble without losing the moment.

A09.q: The StudioBinder video on Walter Murch lists six things an editor weighs when choosing a cut. Which one does Murch rank lowest, and give up first?
options: Keeping where people stand in the space consistent across the cut.
Making sure the cut moves the story forward in a clear, simple way.
Murch ranks story second, just below emotion, so it is near the top.
Making the cut land at a good moment in the scene's rhythm.
Rhythm comes third for Murch, well above matching the space.
Making the cut feel true to the emotion in the scene.
Murch ranks emotion first; it is the last thing he gives up.
A09.why: Murch's rule of six puts emotion first and keeping the space consistent last. If a cut feels true, viewers rarely notice small spatial mismatches.
A09.video: The Book Every Editor Has to Read — Walter Murch and In the Blink of an Eye

A09.q: Your wedding film switches between the baraat arriving and the bride waiting upstairs. When is the best moment to switch from the baraat to the bride?
options: When the procession stops at the gate and the outcome is open.
After the baraat sequence has fully finished playing out.
Finishing one thread completely removes the pull that makes switching worthwhile.
Every few seconds, so both threads stay equally fresh.
Switching that fast is hard to follow and each cut loses its effect.
As soon as the bride finishes getting ready upstairs.
Switch while the outcome is still open, not when the other thread has resolved.
A09.why: Leaving one thread at an open moment makes viewers want to return to it. That pull is what makes crosscutting exciting.

A09.q: A client film moves between a Nashik grape farmer's dawn and a Mumbai buyer's morning. Test viewers say it is confusing. What do you change?
options: Switch less often, and land each switch on a clear link or sharp difference.
Add a text title naming the place and time at every single switch.
Titles label the place but do not fix switches that have no purpose.
Speed up the switches, so the extra energy hides the confusion between places.
Faster switching usually makes a confusing film harder to follow.
Drop the farmer's thread and tell his story in narration.
That removes the contrast the film is built on.
A09.why: Each switch should mean something, such as a matched action or a strong difference between the two lives. Fewer, purposeful switches are easier to follow.

A09.q: In an interview, a mother says, "I never saw him again." Your next clip has music swelling in. How do you handle the cut?
options: Hold a few seconds on her face with only the room's natural sound, then bring in music.
Bring the music in right on her last word, to lift the emotion of the moment for viewers.
Music arriving instantly tells viewers how to feel and steps on her line.
Cut straight to the next interview to keep the pace tight.
Moving on at once gives viewers no time to take in what she said.
Fade the music in slowly from the start of her sentence.
Music under her last words takes attention from them.
A09.why: A short pause with only the quiet natural sound of the place gives the line space to sink in. Music can come after.

A09.q: Watching your rough cut, a client says the four-second pause after the proposal "looks like a mistake." What do you do?
options: Keep the pause, but add room tone and a reaction shot so it feels chosen.
Remove the pause completely so the client stays happy.
Cutting it loses the moment instead of fixing why it felt wrong.
Fill the gap with soft music so there is no dead air.
Music fills the space the pause was meant to give the moment.
Tell the client that long pauses are an artistic choice, and keep the cut as it is.
That ignores the client's concern; make the pause look chosen.
A09.why: Pure digital silence can sound like a dropout, which reads as an error. Room tone (the quiet natural sound of the place) and a reaction shot show the pause is deliberate.

A09.q: Your brand film for a Jaipur jewellery shop runs in order, from raw gold to finished necklace. You think opening on the finished piece might be stronger. Delivery is in two days. What do you do?
options: Copy the sequence, rough out the new order, and watch both versions.
Rebuild the main timeline in the new order and judge it from there.
Working on your only cut risks losing a version that may have been better.
Describe the idea to the client and let them decide before trying it.
Clients judge better from a version they can watch than from a description.
Keep the safer order, since delivery is only two days away.
A copy lets you test the idea safely and quickly.
A09.why: A quick rough version on a copy lets you compare by watching, not guessing. Your original cut stays safe if the new idea does not work.

A09.q: In Inside The Edit's video cutting the same scene two ways, what do the two versions mainly show?
options: The same footage can mean different things based on editing choices.
One version is correct and the other shows common errors.
Both versions are valid; the video compares choices, not right and wrong.
Most of the difference comes from the colour grade and music.
The video focuses on structure, tone, pacing and spacing, not finishing touches.
The second version is a rough cut of the first, with less polish.
Both are finished edits; they differ in order and meaning.
A09.why: By keeping the footage the same, the video isolates decisions about order, tone and spacing. It shows how much the edit itself shapes the story.
A09.video: How Editors Cut the Same Scene in 2 Completely Different Ways

A10.q: You cut an 'umm' out of a shop owner's interview for a small business promo. On headphones you now hear a tiny pop right at the cut. What do you do?
options: Add a very short crossfade across the cut and listen again.
Raise the background music so the pop gets masked.
The pop is still there, and louder music will start to fight the voice.
Run noise reduction over the whole interview clip.
Noise reduction treats steady hiss, not a single click caused by a hard cut.
Delete a frame on each side of the cut and leave it as a hard cut.
A hard cut can still pop; a short crossfade is the fix.
A10.why: A pop at a cut usually comes from the waveform jumping suddenly. A crossfade of a few milliseconds smooths the join so the edit cannot be heard.

A10.q: The workshop treats editing and mixing as separate, deliberate steps. Which order of work does it support?
options: Fix and tidy each clip first, then balance levels across the mix.
Set the final loudness first, then go back and fix each edit.
Any later edit or fix changes the levels, so the loudness work has to be redone.
Add effects to every clip first, then decide what needs fixing.
Processing before listening hides problems and wastes effort on clips that may change.
Mix the levels first, then repair the clips that sound wrong in the mix.
Repair each clip first, then balance them in the mix.
A10.why: Clean, problem-free clips give you a stable base. Balancing comes after, so each decision only has to be made once.

A10.q: A wedding speech has a ceiling fan hum behind it. You open the noise reduction tool. How do you decide on the right setting?
options: Switch the effect on and off while listening to speech on headphones.
Watch the waveform and raise it until the gaps look flat.
A flat-looking waveform tells you nothing about how damaged the voice now sounds.
Listen on your laptop speakers at low volume to judge the overall effect.
Small speakers at low volume hide the swirly artefacts that headphones reveal.
Choose the highest setting and judge it from the waveform only.
Strong settings distort the voice, and the waveform can't show that.
A10.why: Comparing with and without the effect, on headphones, shows the point where the hum drops but the voice still sounds natural. Stop there, even if a little hum remains.

A10.q: Your noise reduction tool asks for a sample of the noise before it works. Which part of the clip do you give it?
options: A few seconds where only the background noise plays, with no speech.
The loudest section of speech, so it learns the voice well.
The tool would treat parts of the voice as noise and remove them.
The whole clip, including the speech and any music.
A mixed sample confuses the tool, so it cuts things you want to keep.
A moment of quiet between two sentences, including the end of the speech.
The sample must have only noise, with no speech.
A10.why: The tool learns what to remove from the sample. A clean noise-only stretch lets it target the hum and leave the voice alone.

A10.q: You tightened a street market interview by cutting pauses. Now the background sound drops to dead silence at every gap. What do you do?
options: Lay a track of room tone under the voice to fill the gaps.
Put the cut pauses back in so the gaps sound normal.
That undoes your edit and brings back the slow pacing you removed.
Raise the music in each gap, so that nobody notices the silence.
The jumps in background sound are still there, and the music now bounces up and down.
Add a long crossfade at each gap to hide the drop.
A crossfade doesn't add the missing room sound.
A10.why: Room tone is a recording of the location with nobody talking. A steady bed of it under the dialogue hides the cuts and keeps the space sounding continuous.

A10.q: The automation lesson covers changing levels over time. Your music should dip whenever the host speaks and rise in the gaps. How do you do it?
options: Draw volume automation that lowers the music under each spoken line.
Lower the music clip once so it stays quiet for the whole film.
The gaps between lines will feel empty and flat with no music lift.
Put a heavy compressor on the music track to keep it down.
A plain compressor evens out the music itself and does not react to the host's speech.
Add a limiter to the music track so it never gets loud.
A limiter doesn't dip the music for the voice.
A10.why: Automation records level moves at exact moments, so the music can step back for speech and come forward between lines.
A10.video: Fundamentals of Mixing Sound in Fairlight — selected lessons

A10.q: In the sound design lesson, effects are added to make scenes feel real. A door slams on screen but there is no sound. What do you do?
options: Add a door effect synced to the frame, at a level that suits the room.
Add the door effect at full level so the moment really stands out.
An effect louder than the scene sounds fake and pulls viewers out of it.
Leave it silent, since the music already carries the moment.
A visible action with no sound feels wrong to viewers, even if they cannot say why.
Add the door effect at the same level as the dialogue.
The effect should match the room, not compete with speech.
A10.why: Good sound design matches timing and level to what we see, so the effect feels like it was recorded on location.
A10.video: Fundamentals of Mixing Sound in Fairlight — selected lessons

A10.q: A client picked a Hindi film song with lyrics for their corporate film. Under the narration, the sung words clash with the spoken words. What do you suggest?
options: Use an instrumental version of the track while the narrator speaks.
Push the narration louder until it is clearly on top of the singing.
The lyrics still compete for attention, and the voice may start to distort.
Keep it as it is, since the client chose this song.
A good editor explains the problem and offers a fix the client can approve.
Lower the music throughout but keep the sung words.
The sung words still clash with the narration.
A10.why: Sung words and spoken words compete for the same attention. An instrumental keeps the feel of the song without blocking the message.

A10.q: Your narration peaks around −12 dB on the meter. Roughly where should the music peak while the narrator is talking?
options: Around −22 dB or lower, well under the voice.
Around −14 dB, close to the voice so it feels full.
That leaves the music nearly as loud as the voice, so words get lost.
Around −40 dB, so it is almost silent.
At that level the music adds nothing and the film feels empty.
Around −12 dB, the same as the voice.
Equal levels make both hard to follow.
A10.why: A gap of about 10 dB or more keeps every word clear while the music is still felt.

A10.q: You recorded a speaker at a function with a lapel mic. A deep rumble from the generator sits under the voice. Which tool fixes it?
options: An EQ high-pass filter that cuts the lowest frequencies.
A compressor with a fast attack, to hold the deep rumble down.
A compressor controls loudness changes and will not remove a steady low tone.
More recording gain so the voice rises above the rumble.
Raising gain makes the rumble louder by the same amount as the voice.
A de-esser, which calms sharp 's' sounds.
A de-esser handles 's' sounds, not low rumble.
A10.why: Rumble lives in very low frequencies the voice barely uses. A high-pass filter around 80 Hz removes it without hurting speech.

A10.q: After compressing a narration, the breaths between lines are now loud and the voice sounds squashed and lifeless. What do you change?
options: Lower the ratio or raise the threshold so it compresses less.
Add more make-up gain, so the voice sounds fuller and closer again.
Make-up gain lifts everything, including the breaths, and leaves the squashed sound.
Boost the low end with EQ to bring back some body.
EQ changes tone but does not undo the over-compression causing the problem.
Add a de-esser to calm the breaths.
A de-esser works on 's' sounds, not breaths.
A10.why: Too much compression flattens natural ups and downs and drags quiet sounds like breaths up. Easing the ratio or threshold brings the life back.

A10.q: Your brand film for YouTube measures −8 LUFS over the whole video. LUFS is a unit of loudness measured across the full film. What do you do before uploading?
options: Bring the full mix down to about −14 LUFS, with peaks below −1 dB.
Leave it loud so it stands out against other videos.
The platform will turn it down anyway, and the over-squashed sound will remain.
Lower each clip until the meter never goes above −14 dB.
That mixes up peak level with overall loudness, and the film will end up too quiet.
Bring the whole film down to −24 LUFS, so that it matches broadcast TV.
YouTube's target is about −14; −24 is for broadcast.
A10.why: Platforms like YouTube turn videos to about −14 LUFS. Mixing to it yourself means you control how it sounds, with no surprise turn-down.

A10.q: The finishing lessons cover cleanup and then loudness normalising, which means setting the whole mix to a target level. What should happen before you normalise?
options: Level and clean every clip so the mix is balanced, then normalise the whole.
Normalise every clip on its own to the target before mixing.
Each clip hitting the target alone does not make the full mix land on target.
Normalise first, then do the cleanup and the levelling of each clip afterwards.
Any cleanup after normalising changes the loudness, so the measurement is no longer right.
Normalise only the loudest clips before mixing.
Normalising happens on the whole mix, after cleanup and levelling.
A10.why: Loudness is measured across the finished whole. Balance and cleanup must be done first, so the final step only sets the overall level.
A10.video: Fundamentals of Mixing Sound in Fairlight — selected lessons

A11.q: You are grading a wedding film. Clips came from a Sony shooting S-Log3, an iPhone recording HLG, and a drone in its normal profile. What do you do before any grading?
options: Give each clip its own camera's input setting so all of them land in one shared space.
Apply one popular LUT to every clip so they all start looking similar.
A LUT made for one camera will push the other cameras' footage the wrong way.
Grade the iPhone clips first by eye, then copy those same settings across onto all the rest.
Each camera stores colour differently, so copied settings will not land the same.
Grade the drone clips first, then match the Sony and iPhone clips to them.
Without the right input settings, matching is guesswork.
A11.why: When the software knows each source, all clips arrive in one shared space. Then your grade behaves the same on every camera.

A11.q: A client sends a clip with no metadata. You cannot tell which camera profile it used. What does the colorist suggest?
options: Try the likely input options and keep the one where greys and contrast look natural.
Leave the input unset and fix everything later with saturation and curves.
Skipping the input step means you fight the wrong starting point in every later node.
Always treat unknown footage as the camera log format that most people use today.
A guess without testing can be badly wrong and break skin and highlights.
Ask the client to resend the clip until it includes metadata.
Clients usually can't add it; test the likely options.
A11.why: Unknown sources need a careful test. Natural neutrals and sensible contrast are the best signs of the right choice.
A11.video: The Pro Colorist Guide to Color Management in 2024

A11.q: Your film will play on YouTube and also on a projector at the reception. How do you handle the two deliveries?
options: Keep one grade and change only the final transform for each screen.
Change the timeline working space for each screen, then touch up the grade.
The working space should stay fixed, or your grade shifts every time you change it.
Build a fresh grade from scratch for each screen the film will play on.
Regrading from zero wastes time when a correct output transform handles most of it.
Use one grade for both screens and let the projector handle the difference.
The projector can't know your grade; set a final transform for each.
A11.why: A managed pipeline keeps the grade in one working space. Only the last step changes for each screen.

A11.q: You grade a shot of a bride in a bright red saree. On the vectorscope the trace stretches far toward red, past the target box. What does this tell you?
options: The red is very saturated and may smear or clip, so pull it back a little.
The red is too bright, so lower the exposure of the whole shot.
The vectorscope does not show brightness; that is the waveform's job.
The shot is fine, because a longer trace simply means richer colour.
Going past the target boxes often means colour that breaks up on screens and on TV.
The red hue is wrong and needs rotating towards orange.
Reaching far from the centre shows strength, not hue.
A11.why: Distance from the centre shows how strong a colour is. A trace past the boxes is a warning to reduce saturation.

A11.q: You shoot a plain grey wall in a shop. On the vectorscope the small blob sits off the centre, toward orange. What does that mean?
options: The shot has a warm cast, so fix white balance until the blob is centred.
The wall is too dark, so raise lift (the shadow level) until it moves.
Lift changes brightness, while the blob's position shows a colour cast.
The wall has strong colour, so boost saturation to match the scope.
A grey wall should have no colour, so more saturation makes the cast worse.
The wall's brightness is wrong, so lift the highlights.
The scope shows colour, not brightness.
A11.why: Neutral greys and whites should sit in the centre of the vectorscope. Any pull to one side is a colour cast.

A11.q: You cut a two-camera interview for a small sweet shop. Camera B looks cooler and slightly green next to Camera A. How do you match them?
options: Pick A as the reference, then adjust B while comparing both side by side on scopes.
Grade each camera on its own until each one looks good by itself.
Two shots can each look fine alone and still jump when cut together.
Grade B until it looks right on the edit monitor, looking at one shot at a time.
Without a side-by-side reference, your eye adjusts and small differences stay hidden.
Make B cooler still, then warm both with one look.
Making it worse and warming both only hides the difference.
A11.why: Matching works best against a fixed reference. Side-by-side viewing and scopes show differences your eye misses.

A11.q: Before you use Color Match to match two shots, what should already be in place?
options: Each clip's colour settings set correctly, so both shots sit in the same space.
A strong creative look on the reference shot, so the match copies it.
Matching works better on balanced shots, with the look added after.
Extra saturation on both shots, so the tool has more colour to read.
Boosting colour first gives the match tool a false picture of the shots.
Leave each camera's log settings as they are, so the colour can be matched later on.
Both shots must sit in the same space first.
A11.why: Auto matching needs a controlled starting point. If clips are interpreted wrongly, the match chases the wrong numbers.
A11.video: Create a professional look using Color Match and Curves

A11.q: After Color Match, the shots are close but the shadows still feel different. What do you do next?
options: Fine-tune with Curves, adjusting the shadow area until the two cuts sit together.
Run Color Match again and again until the shadows happen to line up.
Repeating the same automatic step rarely fixes one tonal range.
Accept it, because the automatic match is always more accurate than your own eye can be.
Auto tools give a starting point, and a working colorist still finishes by hand.
Add more saturation to the shadows of the second shot.
Saturation doesn't match shadow brightness.
A11.why: The match gets you close. Curves let you correct a specific tonal range that the match did not fix.
A11.video: Create a professional look using Color Match and Curves

A11.q: Client notes on a street market shot: the grass is a bit yellow, the whole shot is too dark, and a sign in the back is distracting. Which do you tackle first?
options: The darkness, because changing it shifts how every other part looks.
The yellow grass first, because it is the most obvious problem in the frame.
Lifting the exposure later will change the grass again, so you redo the work.
The distracting sign, because it will take the longest to fix.
How long a fix takes does not decide the order; what it affects does.
Start with the client's list in the order they wrote it.
The order of the notes isn't the order of the work.
A11.why: An exposure change touches every pixel, including the grass and the sign. Doing it first keeps your later small fixes accurate.

A11.q: A wedding shot is already balanced. The client now wants the garden grass a little greener. What do you do?
options: Use a qualifier (a tool that selects by colour) to pick just the greens.
Shift the whole image toward green with the main colour wheel.
That turns skin and the white decor green as well.
Raise overall saturation until the grass looks as green as wanted.
Skin and clothing get too strong long before the grass is right.
Mask the grass with a shape and colour it green.
A shape selects by area, not by colour.
A11.why: Once the base is balanced, small requests need small tools. A qualifier changes one colour range and leaves the rest.

A11.q: At a sangeet under mixed LED lights, faces look slightly pink. On the vectorscope the face area sits off toward magenta. What do you do?
options: Select just the skin and rotate its hue back toward orange, then check by eye.
Lower the saturation of the whole shot until the faces stop looking pink.
This dulls the whole frame and the hue of the skin is still wrong.
Add warmth to the whole frame until the faces look more orange.
Warming moves the decor and clothes too, and does not remove a magenta tint.
Cool the whole frame until the faces stop looking pink.
That changes the colour of everything in the shot.
A11.why: Skin needs the right hue first. Moving only the skin back toward the skin-tone line fixes faces without hurting the rest.

A11.q: A festival group shot has people with very fair and very deep skin. On the vectorscope how should you treat them?
options: Keep every face at a similar hue, and let brightness and saturation differ.
Brighten the darker faces until every face looks about the same tone.
This changes how people really look, and clients will notice and dislike it.
Give each person a different hue so the range of skin reads clearly.
Human skin shares a similar hue, so spreading hues makes some faces look ill.
Pull every face to the same brightness and saturation.
People's faces differ; keep hue similar and let the rest vary.
A11.why: Skin of every tone has a similar hue. What changes is brightness and saturation, so respect those differences.

A11.q: You export a corporate film. On the client's laptop it looks lighter and washed out compared to your timeline. What do you do first?
options: Check the file's colour and gamma tags, then test on the client's kind of screen.
Add contrast to the grade so the export looks richer on their laptop.
This fixes one screen and breaks every other screen the film plays on.
Tell the client their laptop is not calibrated, and send them the same file again.
Most viewers use normal screens, so the delivery must look right on them.
Export in a different container (MOV) and hope it displays correctly.
The container doesn't fix the colour tags.
A11.why: A shift like this is usually a settings mismatch, not a grading problem. Gamma tags tell players how to show brightness, so find the wrong setting, then test on real screens.

A11.q: Your film will play on a hall projector at the reception and later on Instagram. The deadline is tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Export a short test clip and watch it on that projector and on a phone.
Trust your edit monitor, since the grade looked right to you while you worked.
Projectors and phones show colour differently, so problems appear only on them.
Export one final file at the highest bitrate and send it to both.
A high bitrate does not fix colour or brightness differences between screens.
Export two versions, one for each screen, without testing them.
You still have to test on the real screens.
A11.why: Only the real screen tells you how the film will look. A short test saves you from surprises on the day.

A11.q: In the AI Magic Mask tutorial, what do you check before grading inside the mask?
options: The tracking and edges across the whole shot.
Only the first frame.
Masks can slip later in the shot.
Nothing. AI masks are always clean.
Fast movement and hair often cause problems.
Only the brightest part of the shot, where the face is.
The mask must be good across the whole shot.
A11.why: Check the mask through the whole shot first.
A11.video: AI Magic Mask Tutorial: Using a Real Netflix Show

A11.q: You brighten a face with an AI mask. Halfway through, the brightness spills onto the wall. What happened?
options: The mask lost track and needs fixing in that part of the shot.
The grade is too strong for that shot and needs turning down overall.
The problem is where the mask is, not how strong the grade is.
The footage is damaged and the shot needs re-exporting.
The footage is fine. The mask moved.
Your mask edge is too soft and the grade is too strong.
The mask lost track; softness is not the cause.
A11.why: Fix the mask before you judge the grade.

A12.q: You shot a jewellery ad in 4K at 50fps. The broadcaster's sheet asks for 1920x1080, 25fps, ProRes and -24 LUFS loudness (a standard measure of overall volume). What do you send?
options: A 1080p, 25fps ProRes file at -24 LUFS, matching the sheet item by item.
The 4K 50fps file, since higher quality gives them more room to work.
Broadcasters reject files that don't match the sheet, even if the quality is higher.
A 1080p 25fps file mixed louder than asked, so the ad stands out.
Missing the loudness target can get the file rejected or turned down automatically.
A 1080p 25fps H.264 file at a high bitrate, since it plays anywhere.
The sheet asks for ProRes.
A12.why: Clients and broadcasters build their systems around the numbers they give you. Match each one exactly, and ask in writing about anything unclear.

A12.q: A client has agreed to three versions: a TV master, a YouTube file and a small preview. How does the Adobe video suggest you handle this at export?
options: Set up each version as its own export, with the settings agreed for it.
Export one high quality master and let the client convert the rest.
The client paid for three ready files, and their conversions may break the agreed settings.
Use one preset for all three and give each file a different name.
The same settings can't meet three different sets of requirements.
Export a master and make the preview from it, leaving YouTube as the master file.
Each version needs its own settings.
A12.why: The export workflow lets you build each agreed version on purpose. That way every file matches its own requirements.

A12.q: A restaurant wants a YouTube film and some vertical Reels, all cut from one day of shooting on a wide camera. How do you frame on the day?
options: Keep key action near the centre with space around it, so a tall crop still works.
Frame tightly for the wide film, and sort out the vertical cuts later in the edit.
Tight wide framing often leaves nothing usable when you crop to vertical.
Turn the main camera sideways for the whole shoot to suit the Reels.
This ruins the YouTube film to serve the smaller deliverable.
Frame only for the vertical Reels, since they get more views.
The wide film needs its own framing too.
A12.why: Planning for the narrow frame while shooting wide lets one shoot serve both. The crop has room to move without losing faces or products.

A12.q: After an automatic reframe to vertical, a speaker's face slides half out of frame when she leans to one side. What does the video show you should do?
options: Fix that shot by hand with keyframes, markers that set position and size over time.
Leave it, since the automatic tool already tracked the shot for you.
Auto tools make mistakes, and a half-cut face looks careless to viewers.
Put the wide shot inside the vertical frame, with black bars above and below it.
Black bars waste most of the vertical screen and look out of place on Reels.
Run the automatic reframe again at a slower tracking speed.
It may still lose her face; adjust by hand.
A12.why: The automatic pass is only a starting point. Position and scale keyframes let you correct the shots it gets wrong.
A12.video: Reframe your video for multiple social platforms

A12.q: An NGO's YouTube documentary has Hindi interviews. Viewers should be able to read it in English, Tamil or Hindi. You'll use .srt files (plain text subtitle files). What do you deliver?
options: One video with no text in the picture, plus one .srt file for each language.
One video with English burned in, plus Tamil and Hindi .srt files.
Tamil and Hindi viewers would see English text under their own, and no one can hide it.
One clean video plus a single .srt file with all three languages stacked.
Viewers would see three lines at once and can't choose just their language.
Three separate videos, one per language, each with burned-in captions.
Burned-in captions can't be switched off.
A12.why: Separate files per language let each viewer pick one or hide them all. The clean master also stays ready for any future use.

A12.q: A sweet shop wants an Instagram Reel. Most people will scroll past it with the sound off. How do you handle captions?
options: Put the captions into the picture itself, placed clear of the app's buttons.
Upload the Reel with a separate .srt file attached for viewers.
Social feeds often ignore or hide subtitle files, so muted viewers may see nothing.
Skip the captions, because the food shots tell the story well without any words.
Offers and shop details spoken aloud are lost on muted viewers.
Put the captions in the post's description instead.
Captions in a description aren't read with the video.
A12.why: On muted social feeds, captions fixed in the picture are the only ones everyone will see. Keep them away from the like and comment buttons.

A12.q: You've exported a corporate film and the deadline is in 40 minutes. The timeline looked fine all day. What do you do before sending?
options: Play the exported file in full in a separate player, with headphones on.
Scrub through the timeline once more to confirm the edit is right.
The timeline is not the export, and some errors appear only in the rendered file.
Open the file, check the first and last minute, then send it.
Audio drops or a missing graphic can hide anywhere in the middle.
Check the file size and length in the file details.
Size and length don't show picture or sound problems.
A12.why: Export can add problems the timeline never showed. Watching the actual file in full, against the spec, is the only way to know what the client will get.

A12.q: While checking the final file, you notice the interview voice plays only in your left headphone. What do you do?
options: Set the dialogue to play in both channels, export again and recheck the file.
Send it anyway, since most people watch on phone speakers.
Many viewers use earphones, and one-sided voice sounds broken to them.
Raise the overall volume, so the voice is clear enough coming from just one side.
Louder audio doesn't fix the channel problem and may break the loudness target.
Switch the headphones to mono and send the file.
Mono hides the problem but doesn't fix the left-only audio.
A12.why: A mono voice placed on one side is a common export fault. Fix the routing, then check the new file again, because every fix can add a new error.

A12.q: You're sending a hotel client the third cut of their vertical promo. Which file name do you use?
options: Hotel_Promo_9x16_v03_2026-03-04.mp4
Hotel_Promo_v03_04-03-2026_final.mp4
It leaves out the shape, and a day-first date won't sort in order.
Hotel_Promo_9x16_v03_FINAL.mp4
There is no date, and FINAL becomes false if the client asks for another round.
Hotel_Promo.mp4
It doesn't show the version, shape or date.
A12.why: Shape, version number and a year-month-day date tell anyone what the file is, and the files sort in the right order.

A12.q: A client left timecoded notes on your first cut in Frame.io. You've made the fixes. How does the video show you should upload the new cut?
options: Add it as a new version on the same item, so notes and cuts stay together.
Upload it as a separate file and email the client the new link.
The notes stay on the old file, so no one can easily check what was fixed.
Delete the first cut and upload the new one fresh to avoid confusion.
Deleting it throws away the record of what the client asked for.
Send the new cut as a link to a file on your own drive.
The client's notes stay with the version on Frame.io.
A12.why: Stacking versions keeps each comment linked to the cut it was about. You and the client can compare and confirm each fix.
A12.video: Enhance your review process with Frame.io

A12.q: A wedding film is delivered and your drive is nearly full. You must free space, but you may need to re-edit next year. What do you remove?
options: The render and preview cache files.
The original camera footage files, all of them.
Without the originals you can never re-edit or make a new version.
The edit project file.
The project file holds every edit decision and takes very little space.
The graphics and title templates.
You need those to re-edit.
A12.why: Cache files are rebuilt automatically from the footage and project. The originals, project and masters can't be replaced if lost.

A12.q: The WITNESS video talks about planning to keep footage safe for years. What is the key step it points to?
options: Decide who is responsible for the footage and keep copies in separate places.
Keep it on your own laptop, since you shot it and know the files best.
One copy on one device can be lost to theft, damage or failure.
Leave it on the cloud service you used to share it with the team.
Sharing services can delete files, close accounts or change rules without warning.
Copy it to a USB stick and keep it in your bag.
One copy in one place isn't safe.
A12.why: Long-term safety needs a named person in charge and copies stored in different places. Without both, footage quietly disappears.
A12.video: Planning to Preserve Video for Human Rights

A13.q: Before a big wedding project, you pick a highly praised wedding film to learn from. How do you study it?
options: Rewatch it scene by scene and write down why each part moves you.
Copy its shot list and song choices closely for your next wedding couple.
Copying gives you their film for a different couple, not a skill you can reuse.
Find out which camera and lenses they used and rent the same kit.
Their kit is the smallest part of why the film works, so it teaches you very little.
Watch it once for fun, then copy its first and last scenes.
Copying scenes teaches nothing about why they work.
A13.why: Breaking a film into scenes and asking why each one lands teaches you the craft behind it. You can then use those reasons in your own way.

A13.q: When you study how a skilled editor builds a film in your style, what is the most useful thing to look at first?
options: How the story and the music decide the order of the moments.
Which transitions and effects they use between the clips.
Transitions are surface polish and cannot hold up a film with a weak structure.
Which colour grade preset gives their footage its look.
A grade changes the look, but it does not make the film coherent or moving.
Note which camera angles they use at each moment.
Angles are a result; learn why the story and music pick them.
A13.why: A strong film is built on story and music before anything else. Once you see that foundation, the other choices make sense.

A13.q: You watch an experienced filmmaker cover a one-time live event like a ceremony. What is the best way to critique their setup?
options: Note where each camera and mic sits, and what is lost if one fails.
Note how many cameras they own and plan to buy the same number.
The number of cameras matters less than how each one is placed and used.
Note only the look of the main camera, since that is what clients see.
A live event depends on the full plan, including backup angles and clean sound.
Compare how it looks on a big screen and on a phone.
That says nothing about how the setup holds up if something fails.
A13.why: A ceremony happens once, so a good plan covers every angle and sound source. Asking what fails if one piece drops shows how strong the plan really is.
A13.video: How to Film a Wedding Ceremony

A13.q: At a pre-wedding shoot in Udaipur, the couple look stiff and awkward on camera. What do you do?
options: Ask them to walk toward you while she tells him a funny story.
Tell them to relax, be natural and just look happy together for the camera.
Vague instructions make people more self-aware, so they usually get stiffer.
Show them poses on your phone and ask them to hold each one.
Held poses often look forced and leave you with stills, not moving moments.
Give them a script of lines to say to each other.
Scripted lines make a stiff couple stiffer.
A13.why: People look natural when they are busy doing something real. A simple task gives them something to focus on other than the camera.

A13.q: A textile shop owner in Jaipur wants a brand film and asks you to start shooting tomorrow with no prep. What do you do?
options: Take a day to outline the story, list the shots and walk him through it.
Start filming everything in the shop and find the story in the edit.
Shooting without a story wastes time and often misses the shots the film needs.
Write a full script with lines for the owner to learn by heart.
Non-actors reading memorised lines usually sound wooden on camera.
Agree to start tomorrow, and do the outline over the weekend afterwards instead.
The outline is needed before shooting.
A13.why: A short outline (often called a treatment) and a shot list keep the shoot focused. A quick walk-through means everyone knows what to do on the day.

A13.q: At a sangeet, the bride's family will perform one big dance. You are alone with two cameras. How do you set up?
options: Lock one camera on a wide of the stage and handhold the other for faces.
Use both cameras for close-ups so you capture every small detail.
With no wide shot, you have nothing to cut back to when a close-up misses.
Set one camera to slow motion and shoot the dance with the other.
Slow motion is a nice extra, but it leaves the main dance with only one usable angle.
Use both cameras handheld for medium shots and switch in the edit.
You'd have no safe wide shot of the whole dance.
A13.why: The locked wide makes sure the whole dance is recorded, and the handheld camera adds emotion. Together they give the edit what it needs.

A13.q: You are filming a company founder's interview and only 20 minutes are left. What do you shoot?
options: Re-ask her main questions from a second angle, then record room sound.
A time-lapse of the busy office lobby to open the film.
A time-lapse is a nice extra, while the interview is what the film depends on.
Slow-motion shots of the company logo on the wall behind reception.
Logo shots can be grabbed any time, but her answers cannot be redone easily.
Close-up cutaways of the founder's hands and workspace.
Her interview is the part that can't be repeated.
